aaliyah.text: Aaliyah's arc is almost entirely explained by one person. The singer Aaliyah, born 1979, died in 2001, and the name reached its highest birth count of 5,522 and best rank of 36 in 2012 — a delayed peak rather than an immediate one, which is the usual shape when a name is carried by memory instead of active fame. A 45% drop since then brings it to 2,703 births and rank 93. The name entered American data in 1976, three years before the singer, and has accumulated 107,420 births, the overwhelming majority after 1994. Of Arabic origin and with exactly one recorded bearer, this is about as clean a case of single-person attribution as the dataset contains — and the decline that follows is equally characteristic.

aaron.text:
15,311 in 1989 marks Aaron's biggest year by count; the rank caught up five years later, reaching #28 in 1994. Both have receded since — 4,225 births and #79 in 2024, 43% down from what it counted a decade back.

Six hundred thousand-plus US births trace to this name since 1880, a solid mid-tier history — not among the dataset's largest names, but no recent arrival either.

Aaron Swartz, Aaron Burr, and Nobel-winning biologist Aaron Klug share almost nothing career-wise beyond this one name spanning tech activism, early American politics, and science.

abigail.text:
Abigail posted the steepest ten-year decline in this batch: down 55% to 5,499 births in 2024, landing at #32. Its rank peaked at #4 in 2005, two years after the raw count's own high of 15,932 births in 2003.

The enrichment data lists no famous bearers at all, despite the name's biblical origin and its earlier run near the top of the chart — a gap shared with Penelope and Zoe elsewhere in this batch.

That combination — a rapid, recent fall from a genuine top-five position, and no documented namesake pulling in the other direction — makes Abigail's decline look less like a slow fade and more like a sharp reversal with nothing currently working to offset it.

adam.text:
Adam's rank peaked a year before its count did: #18 in 1983, then 23,940 births the following year, 1984 — a tight one-year gap. The name has fallen 35% since a decade ago, to 3,497 births and #100 in 2024.

This name's own total, 578,925 births since 1880, is a substantial historical footprint.

Economist Adam Smith anchors the name in 18th-century political thought, while comedian Adam Sandler keeps it current — and the enrichment data even lists the biblical first man himself, with no birth year attached at all.

addison.text:
Addison ties Jaxon for the steepest decline in this batch, both down 53% across the last ten years. Both measures hit their high point together in 2007 — 11,949 births, #11 nationally, a genuine near-top-ten run — before falling to 3,327 births and #68 by 2024.

There's no history here before 1980 at all, unusual for this range of the dataset — a full century of the dataset with no recorded births under this name.

TikTok star Addison Rae is the standout contemporary bearer, alongside former US Secretary of State James Baker, whose middle name was Addison.

adeline.text:
143% growth over the past decade puts Adeline among the bigger jumps in this range, its total US births now past 76,951 since the name entered the data in 1880 — bringing it to a fresh 2024 peak: 3,723 births, #58 nationally. The actual high-water mark for raw count came earlier, 4,119 in 2016.

Records run the dataset's full length, from 1880 onward.

Virginia Woolf's middle name was Adeline, a literary connection dating to the 1880s; amateur wrestler Adeline Gray brings the name into recent Olympic sport.

adrian.text:
Adrian's count and rank peaked together in 2008 — 7,937 births and #56 nationally — a clean simultaneous high.

Since then the decline has been steady rather than sharp: 4,617 births in 2024, down 31% from a decade prior, landing at #72.

The bearer list here is unusually international for this batch — Romanian footballer Adrian Mutu, British double agent Kim Philby (born Harold Adrian Russell Philby), German Formula One driver Adrian Sutil — a name whose public figures span at least four countries without concentrating in any one.

adriel.text:
A 368% surge over the last ten years — one of the largest jumps in this batch — brought Adriel to 3,248 births in 2024, a record matched by its best-ever rank, #109.

Just 30,803 people have ever carried this name in the US, dating only to 1952, a small enough base to help explain such a large percentage swing, the same shape seen in Thiago's and Luka's own surges from earlier batches.

Nothing turns up in the enrichment data as a namesake.

aiden.text:
Aiden is one of the more recent arrivals in this batch by data history, first appearing only in 1970. Its best-ever rank, #9, came in 2010, a year after the name's raw count itself peaked at 16,029 births in 2009.

The decline since has been sharp: 6,243 births in 2024, 54% under its count from a decade before, landing at #47 — a steeper fall than Mason's or Jacob's tied 62% only by a matter of degree, and one of the fastest reversals in this batch for a name that only recently cracked the top 10.

The enrichment data names just one real namesake here, footballer Aiden McGeady, active since the mid-2000s — a thin cultural anchor for a name whose rise and fall both happened within the same twenty-year window.

ailany.text: Nothing else on this site behaves like Ailany. It is up 7,317% over ten years — not a typo, and roughly seventeen times the next-largest gain in this batch. The mechanics are stark: 4,014 births in total since the name first appeared in 2000, of which 2,596 happened in 2024 alone. Roughly two thirds of everyone ever given this name was born in a single year, taking it straight to rank 101. There are no recorded namesakes and no listed origin. A curve this shape almost always means one moment of mass exposure rather than gradual adoption, but the dataset contains no evidence of what it was, and it would be irresponsible to guess. What can be said is that a name arriving this fast has no track record at all, and names without one are the hardest to predict.

alaia.text: Alaia is the second-most explosive name in these four batches, behind only Ailany: up 3,574% over ten years, to 2,425 births and rank 112, both 2024 records. Its entire recorded history amounts to 15,367 births since 1986, so more than a seventh of everyone ever given the name arrived last year alone. No namesakes and no origin are listed. The couturier Azzedine Alaïa is the obvious association and is absent from the file, spelled with an accent the data would not carry anyway. Two names in one batch showing four-figure percentage growth is unusual, and both share the same profile: no history, no attached person, and a curve that gives a forecaster nothing to work with.

alexander.text:
Alexander's slide is one of the sharpest of any established name in this range — down 51% over the past decade — after dropping from a peak position of #4, its best ever, held in 2009, all the way to #27 by 2024. Its raw-count peak came earlier still, 20,529 births in 1993, meaning the name has now been declining in some form for roughly three decades.

It's been recorded since 1880 and carries a total of 733,348 US births, a large historical base for a name now well outside the top 20.

The famous-bearer list is dense with 19th-century scientists and scholars — Alexander Graham Bell, Alexander von Humboldt, Alexander Fleming — a concentration of invention and discovery that few other names in this batch match, though none of it appears to have slowed the name's recent slide.

alice.text:
Alice's rank hit its best mark, #8, in 1880 — the same year Samuel, John, Thomas, William, Charles, and August also peaked positionally, per earlier batches. The raw count came 41 years later, 11,955 births in 1921.

586,537 total US births since 1880 make this one of the larger names in this batch by history, and the recent trend is mildly positive: up 15% over the past decade to 3,520 births in 2024.

Nobel laureate Alice Munro and activist Alice Walker anchor the name in 20th-century literature; rock musician Alice Cooper, born Vincent Furnier, shows it carried by a man as a stage name.

allison.text: Allison has lost 52% in ten years, from a best rank of 30 in 2009 and a peak count of 8,150 back in 1994, down to 2,622 births at rank 99. Like Sarah and Anna it is paying the price of having been extremely common within recent memory, though its 320,344 births are concentrated in a much narrower window — nothing before 1908, and most of the volume between 1975 and 2010. The bearers are almost entirely American actors: Allison Janney, born 1959, Allison Williams, Allison Mack. Alyson Hannigan, born 1974, appears under a different spelling, and Drew Carey through a middle name. Spelling fragmentation across Allison, Alison, Allyson and Alyson makes the real usage higher than this line suggests, as with Elliot.

amara.text: Amara has grown 277% over the decade and set both records in 2024, on 2,288 births alongside rank 121. The record opens in 1961 and reaches 26,615 births, with no origin given and a single modern namesake who has no evident bearing on the trajectory. The name has independent roots in Igbo, Italian and Sanskrit, none of which the enrichment file captures, and that multiplicity is probably the point — it reads as familiar to families from very different backgrounds without belonging exclusively to any of them. Names that work across several traditions at once have been among the strongest performers of the past decade, and Amara is a cleaner example of the pattern than most.

amari.text:
2,419 births was Amari's peak count, set in 2023, the same year its rank hit its own high, #151. Both eased slightly the following year, to 2,158 births and #172 in 2024 — still 119% above where the name stood a decade earlier.

Amari's own SSA record opens a full century after the dataset itself, in 1974 — total births for the name now stand at 50,446.

No namesake shows up anywhere in the enrichment data, leaving this name's rapid rise with no documented cultural reference to explain it.

amelia.text:
Amelia's birth count peaked in 2021 at 13,032, and its rank reached its own best-ever mark, #3, in 2024 — essentially where it sits now. That's a 45% rise over the past decade, one of the few names in the current top ten still gaining rather than sliding from an earlier high.

Unlike most names in this range, the enrichment data doesn't attach it to a clear linguistic origin, and its most prominent historical namesake, Empress Amélie of Brazil, is a specific royal figure rather than a broad cultural reference point most parents would recognize today. That makes Amelia's rise harder to pin on any single influence.

What the data does show is a name gaining altitude at exactly the moment several -a-ending names (Olivia, Sophia, Isabella) are declining from their own earlier peaks — Amelia's climb looks less like an isolated trend and more like it's catching some of the demand that those names are shedding as parents look for something with a similar sound but less market saturation.

amir.text:
3,625 births and #95 nationally — both records for Amir in 2024, up 99% from ten years before.

The name's US history starts comparatively late, 1954, though its enrichment data reaches much further back: 13th-century poet Amir Khusrau and 7th-century military commander Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah, born the year 583, the second-oldest figures attached to any name in this batch, trailing only Eli's namesake.

Contemporary bearers include footballer Amir Karić and singer known simply as Amir, born Amir Haddad — a name whose modern American use is recent even though its roots run deep.

andrew.text:
Andrew's 57% decline over the past decade ranks second-steepest in this batch, behind Jayden's 60%. Its rank peaked at #5 in 1988, a year after the raw count's own high of 36,205 in 1987.

Its total climbs past 1.3 million births since 1880, a longer, larger history than most of the names surrounding it in this range.

Andy Warhol (born Andrew Warhola), two US presidents (Andrew Jackson, Andrew Johnson), and industrialist Andrew Carnegie span art, politics, and business across two centuries — a name whose historical weight hasn't slowed its recent fall.

angel.text:
Angel's count and rank peaked in the exact same year, 2006 — 11,602 births and #31 nationally — a tidy simultaneous peak, matching the pattern seen in Cameron and Isaiah.

Since then the fall has been sharp in rank terms: down to #63 by 2024, even though the raw-count decline, 21% over the decade, looks comparatively mild next to a name like Abigail's 55% drop.

First recorded in 1888, just eight years into the dataset, Angel's famous-bearer list leans international and contemporary — footballer Angel Gomes, actor Angel Coulby — without any older reference point anchoring the name the way Charles's centuries-old namesakes do.

anna.text: Anna ranked 2 in 1880, the very first year of SSA records, and peaked at 15,666 births in 1918. It now sits at 2,700 births and rank 94, having lost 53% in a decade. The 915,007 births behind it make this one of the most-used girls' names in American history. Its bearers are a strange collection, because Anna is so often a first name hidden behind something else: Eleanor Roosevelt, born 1884, was Anna Eleanor; Tina Turner was born Anna Mae Bullock. The poet Wisława Szymborska and Monica Bellucci also carry it. Very few names can claim continuous top-tier presence from 1880 to the present, and the cost of that longevity is that Anna now reads as belonging to everyone and no one in particular.

anthony.text:
Anthony shows a long lag between its rank and count peaks: the rank hit #7 in 2007, but the raw count had already peaked seventeen years earlier, 25,087 births in 1990 — the opposite direction from Elizabeth's pattern, where rank peaked long before count.

Total births run to 1,489,090 since 1880, and 2024's count of 6,326 is down 46% from a decade prior, landing at #44 — one of the steeper declines among this batch's older, more established names.

Anthony Hopkins, Anthony Bourdain, and wrestler-turned-actor John Cena (born John Felix Anthony Cena) span acting, food media, and sport across recent decades, a namesake list weighted toward the present despite the name's much longer history in the data.

archer.text:
Archer's 162% climb across the last ten years brought it to a fresh 2024 record: 3,093 births, #115 nationally, both new highs, out of a total that now runs to 28,135 since 1880.

Technically present since 1880, though nearly all of this name's volume has landed in just the past few years.

Nobel-winning biochemist Archer John Porter Martin, born 1910, is the only namesake in the enrichment data, a scientific reference from almost a century before the name's own recent rise.

aria.text:
Aria is essentially flat: 0% change over the past ten years, one of the only names across all four batches to land exactly on zero. Its rank peaked at #19 in 2018, the same year the raw count hit its own high of 7,435 — a clean, simultaneous peak with no lag between the two measures.

The name only enters SSA data in 1900, twenty years after the dataset's start, and its enrichment data lists a single bearer, actor Aria Giovanni, whose career doesn't predate the name's own 2010s rise.

That combination — flat growth, a recent single peak, one contemporary namesake — makes Aria one of the more static entries in this batch, neither climbing nor falling in any meaningful way right now.

ariana.text: Ariana peaked on both measures in 2014 — 5,502 births, rank 37 — which is the year after Ariana Grande's first album. It has since given back 53%, to 2,569 births at rank 103. That timing is close enough to be causal, and the subsequent decline follows the familiar shape: a name attached to one very visible person rises fast and then falls as the association hardens. Recorded from 1957, 118,325 births in total. The bearer list is unusually crowded with genuine Arianas — DeBose, Richards, Greenblatt — alongside Tiffany Trump, born 1993, for whom it is a middle name. Compare Aaliyah, whose curve has an almost identical profile for almost identical reasons.

arlo.text: Arlo has grown 379% across the decade and set records in 2024 on both count and rank, at 2,481 births and 146. Against that, its cumulative total is just 22,607 — one of the smallest figures anywhere in this batch, and evidence that the name barely existed in America before about 2010 despite being recorded from 1899. The single listed bearer is Arlo Guthrie, born 1947, whose fame peaked in the late sixties and who therefore cannot explain a rise that started forty years later. Short, ends in a vowel, no formal version required: Arlo shares its structure with Milo and Theo, and the whole group has moved together, which suggests the sound is doing the work rather than any person.

arthur.text:
1880 is when Arthur's rank hit its all-time best, #14 — the same opening year that produced positional peaks for Samuel, John, Thomas, William, Charles, August, and Alice, all covered in earlier batches. The raw count arrived on its own schedule, 41 years afterward: 10,527 births in 1921.

548,057 total births carry this name across that span, and lately it's been climbing fast — 188% growth over the past decade, a rare growth spurt for a name this historically large.

Philosopher Bertrand Russell and science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke anchor it in 20th-century thought; King Charles III has it tucked into his own name as a middle name, linking the British monarchy to this same word.

asher.text:
Asher is still on its way up: an 87% rise over the past decade brought it to its highest-ever rank, #20, in 2022, and 2024's count of 8,123 sits only slightly below that peak of 8,410 — a name that hasn't yet shown any sign of turning over.

Its history in the data has real gaps: the decades-active list skips the 1900s entirely, meaning fewer than five Asher births were recorded in the US in that decade, before the name picked back up in the 1910s and has appeared in every decade since — an unusually specific dormant stretch for a name with roots this old (first recorded in 1880).

Its famous-bearer list is a mix of the historical and the very recent — 19th-century painter Asher Brown Durand, playwright Arthur Miller (born Asher Miller), and Disney Channel actor Asher Angel — which, unlike Michael's steady multi-century presence, looks more like a name that went quiet for most of its history and only recently found an audience.

ashley.text: Ashley was the single most popular girls' name in America during 1991, and its busiest year for births was 1987 at 54,853 — the second-highest single-year figure across these four batches, behind only Jason. It has since fallen to 2,231 births at rank 124, off 37% in the past decade alone. Cumulative total 873,844, recorded from 1917 with a gap in the 1920s. The bearers divide neatly by sex and nationality: the American Ashleys are women, including Ashley Judd, born 1968, and Ashley Tisdale, while the British ones are male footballers, Ashley Cole and Ashley Young. Halsey, born 1994, is Ashley Frangipane. A name that reached number one this recently carries an almost unusable generational stamp.

athena.text: Athena has exactly one recorded namesake, and she is a child: Countess Athena of Monpezat, born 2012, a member of the Danish royal family. For a name given to 2,788 American girls last year, that is a startlingly thin association — the Greek goddess is doing all the work, and she is not in the file. Growth has been strong at 65% over the decade, with the best rank of 76 arriving in 2023 and the highest birth count in 2022. The name entered American records in 1902 and has gathered 50,614 births since, nearly all of them recent. Mythological names for girls have moved as a group, alongside Luna and Aurora, and Athena's particular appeal is that it comes with a ready-made character rather than just a sound.

atlas.text:
731% growth across the last ten years is the largest gain in this batch, though still short of Lainey's 901% record from the fifth batch. That climb took Atlas to a fresh 2024 high: 3,417 births, #101 nationally.

The name has technically been present since 1883, just three years into the dataset, though almost all its volume has arrived in the last several years.

No namesake appears anywhere in the enrichment data — a name borrowed directly from Greek mythology rather than from any individual who's carried it.

aubrey.text: No name in this batch has fallen further than Aubrey: down 71% in ten years, from rank 15 and 8,059 births in 2012 to 2,209 births at rank 130. Reaching the top fifteen and then losing seven-tenths of your volume within a decade is a violent arc, and it usually indicates a name that arrived on a specific wave. Recorded from 1889 with 162,498 births. The file is a good illustration of how these lists mislead: its highest-profile entry is Drake, born 1986, whose given name is Aubrey Drake Graham and who has never gone by it. Aubrey Plaza and the illustrator Aubrey Beardsley, born 1872, are the genuine bearers, and the name has also shifted decisively from male to female along the way.

audrey.text: Audrey's decline is steeper than its reputation suggests. Down 46% over ten years, from a 2015 high of 5,613 births to 2,993 now, with rank slipping from a 2013 best of 33 to 82. That is the second-largest fall in this batch after Nicholas, and it has happened quietly, because the name still reads as timeless rather than dated. Audrey Hepburn, born 1929, anchors the association so completely that the other listed bearers — Audrey Tautou, Audrey Tang, Audrey Azoulay — barely register by comparison. The file also includes Audre Lorde, born 1934, spelled without the final letter. Recorded from 1881 onward and 305,866 births deep, Audrey has been continuously available for well over a century, which may be exactly the problem: nothing about it currently feels like a discovery.

august.text:
1880 — the dataset's opening year — is also when August's rank hit its best mark, #74, putting it alongside Samuel, John, Thomas, William, and Charles as names that peaked positionally right at the start. What's stranger: the count record came separately, 144 years later in 2024, at 3,876 births — the name's best year ever, and it still ranks lower today, #88, than it did in 1880.

That record count rides on 151% growth over the past decade — a big jump, though still short of this batch's very top risers, Theo and Walker.

Economist Friedrich Hayek, chemist Svante Arrhenius, and biologist Ernst Haeckel form an unusually academic cluster of 19th- and 20th-century European scholars.

aurora.text:
151% growth over the past decade put Aurora at a fresh peak in both count and rank for 2024 — 6,917 births, #16 nationally — second only to Maverick's gain rate in this batch.

Unlike nearly every other name covered across all three batches so far, the enrichment data has nothing to say about Aurora: no linguistic origin, no famous bearers at all. Its cultural pull, whatever it is, isn't showing up in the reference data the way Violet's or Hazel's does.

That blank slate makes it hard to attribute the rise to any specific influence. What the birth data does confirm is the shape of the climb: present since 1880 but essentially flat for more than a hundred years before this recent, sharp acceleration.

austin.text:
Austin's rank peaked a year after its count did: 25,907 births in 1995, then #9 the following year, 1996 — among the highest ranks reached by any name in this batch. Since then, a 48% fall over the past decade landed it at 3,290 births and #107 in 2024, out of a total that's reached 440,461 since 1880 — a substantial name by history, even well outside today's top 50.

Post Malone, born Austin Richard Post, and actor Austin Butler keep the name visible in music and film; 19th-century painter Edwin Austin Abbey shows it carried as a middle name well over a century earlier.

autumn.text: Autumn splits its two peaks by fifteen years: most births in 1998 at 4,208, best rank in 2013 at 64. A name can climb the rankings while producing fewer babies, and this is a clean example. Currently at 3,030 births and rank 79, down 26% across the decade. As a word-name it belongs to a category that behaves differently from inherited names — no saint, no president, no long line of bearers to anchor it. The data reflects that. It first appears in 1910 and the enrichment file offers a single namesake, the actor Autumn Reeser, born 1980, who postdates the name's American rise rather than causing it. Season names tend to arrive with a decade and leave with it; a 143,464 all-time total suggests Autumn has done better than most at avoiding that.

ava.text:
Ava peaked in 2007 at 18,053 births and has fallen sharply since, down 45% over the past decade to 8,662 in 2024 — the steepest decline of any name in this batch, dropping from a best-ever rank of #3 in 2016 to #9 today.

It's been in SSA records since 1880 but, like several names in this group, spent most of that history in minor use before a rapid rise beginning in the 2000s — meaning its current decline is really the back half of a fairly short, sharp cycle rather than a long slow fade.

Ava Gardner's mid-20th-century fame predates the name's actual popularity boom by half a century, which suggests the name's recent rise wasn't really about her; its shorter, punchier famous-bearer list (singer Ava Max, director Ava DuVernay) reflects a name whose visible cultural presence caught up with its birth-record popularity only after the fact rather than driving it.

avery.text:
Avery's data starts in 1890, a decade later than most of its neighbors in this batch but well before recent arrivals like Dylan (1953) or Harper (1971).

Its rank peaked at #12 in 2013, one year ahead of its raw-count peak of 9,578 in 2014 — the peak-then-count pattern seen in a few other names here, just reversed in order. By 2024 its count had dropped to 5,632, a 41% decline over ten years that left it at #31 — one of the steeper drops in this batch alongside David's and Joseph's.

Its famous-bearer list is entirely contemporary and entertainment-adjacent — actors Bella Thorne and Troian Bellisario, singer Grace VanderWaal — young public figures rather than any older reference point, fitting a name whose current form of popularity is a relatively recent development despite its longer data history.

axel.text:
4,666 was Axel's peak count, set in 2020; #71, its best rank, took three more years to arrive, in 2023. It's eased slightly since, to 4,245 births and #78 by 2024, still up 51% from a decade earlier.

SSA records for this name stretch back to 1880, mostly quiet until the current run.

Norwegian king Haakon VII, poet Erik Axel Karlfeldt, and 17th-century statesman Axel Oxenstierna root the name deep in Nordic history, alongside contemporary footballer Axel Witsel and Belgian personal physician Axel Munthe, whose memoir remained a bestseller for decades.

ayla.text:
Up 173% over the past decade, Ayla hit 3,236 births in 2024 — a fresh high matched by its best-ever rank, #69.

The dataset's first eight decades pass with no record of this name at all; it first appears in 1963, with total US births now standing at 34,866.

No documented namesake exists anywhere in the enrichment data for this one, and no origin is listed either — a name whose 173% climb has left no traceable cultural footprint behind it at all.

beau.text:
Beau's growth, 187% over the past decade, brought both its count and rank to new highs together in 2024: 4,694 births at #69.

Its data history is shorter than most names in this range — the first recorded year is 1932, more than five decades after the dataset's 1880 start.

Beau Biden, son of the former president, is the most politically visible bearer, alongside actor Beau Bridges — a small but concentrated namesake list for a name still relatively new to significant popularity.

beckett.text: Beckett reached 2,186 births and rank 166 in 2024, both bests, on 43% growth over ten years — modest against everything else here, where several names have tripled. Recorded from 1992, 27,893 births in total, no origin listed and no namesakes at all. Samuel Beckett is the association most people would name and is absent from the file, which is consistent: these lists index people whose given name matches, not people whose surname supplied the fashion. That is the whole story of this cohort. Beckett, Sutton and Beckham are all surnames repurposed as first names, and the literary or athletic figures behind them never appear in the data precisely because they carried them the other way round.

beckham.text: Beckham's record is the most broken in these four batches by a distance: recorded in 1902, after which eight of the twelve decades that follow are simply blank, the name vanishing for most of the twentieth century before returning. It has grown 279% over the decade to reach 2,180 births and rank 168 in 2024, both bests, on a cumulative total of 18,397. No namesakes are listed, which is almost comic given that the name's entire American existence is attributable to one footballer who carried it as a surname. That is the structural blind spot in this data: it can only see people whose given name matches, so the single most important figure behind a name like this is invisible by design.

bella.text: The bearer file for Bella includes Bella Swan, the protagonist of Twilight, recorded as a high school student born in 1987 — the third fictional character to appear in these lists, after Tom Cat under Jasper and J. Jonah Jameson under Jonah. In this case the fiction is arguably the most relevant entry: the name's peak on both measures, 5,135 births and rank 48, came in 2010, at the height of those films. A 40% fall since then leaves it at 2,469 births and rank 109. Recorded from 1880 but with only 81,582 births total, Bella functions as a short form of Isabella that broke away and now competes with its own parent name for the same children.

benjamin.text:
Benjamin peaked comparatively long ago for a name still in the current top 15: 15,733 births in 1989. From there it's been a slow, multi-decade slide rather than a recent turn — 9,814 births in 2024, 29% below where it stood ten years earlier.

It's been recorded since 1880, giving it well over a century of steady, largely unspectacular use — never a chart-topper like William or James, but rarely absent from the top tier either, a kind of durability without ever needing a single breakout moment.

Its famous-bearer list is dominated by early American figures — Benjamin Franklin, Benjamin Harrison — reflecting the name's deep roots in US naming culture specifically, distinct from names like Mateo or Theodore whose rises are more recent and less tied to any particular national historical figure.

bennett.text:
Bennett's growth rate over the past decade landed on an exact round number: 100%, a straight doubling, bringing both its count and rank to fresh highs in 2024 — 5,095 births at #60 nationally.

Bennett's own SSA data runs back to 1880 too, a long, mostly quiet history before this recent climb.

Its famous-bearer list runs through jazz (Benny Carter, born Bennett Lester Carter), film (director Bennett Miller), and television (actor Ben Savage, born Benjamin Bennett Savage) — three different fields, none of them producing a household name prominent enough to obviously explain the sudden doubling in popularity.

blake.text: Blake has collapsed. Down 74% in ten years — by far the steepest fall anywhere in this batch, and one of the sharpest on the site — from 6,047 births in 2012 at rank 71 to 1,311 today at rank 265. Almost nothing else here has lost that much ground that fast. Part of the explanation is that Blake is genuinely split between boys and girls, so the single line understates the churn happening underneath it. Blake Lively, born 1987, is the most visible bearer and pulled the name toward girls; Blake Griffin and Blake Edwards pull the other way. Recorded from 1883 with 204,479 births banked, most of it accumulated in a twenty-year window either side of that 2012 peak. Unisex names tend to be unstable, and this is what that instability looks like at full scale.

brooklyn.text: Brooklyn is down 64% in ten years, from 7,178 births and rank 21 in 2011 to 2,487 at rank 108. Place-names age quickly, and this one had an unusually sharp arc: the record starting in 1972 and running to 124,665 births, essentially all of them between 1995 and 2015. One bearer is listed, the model Brooklyn Decker, born 1987. Absent from the file, though far more likely to have mattered, is David and Victoria Beckham's eldest son, born 1999 and named for the borough — the timing lines up with the American rise considerably better than Decker does. Names taken from cities carry a specific decade's taste in a way that inherited names do not, and Brooklyn is now firmly stamped with the 2000s.

brooks.text:
Brooks posted a 215% gain over the past decade, with both its count and rank hitting fresh highs together in 2024: 4,793 births at #67.

The name has technically been in SSA data since 1880, though its enrichment list carries only two entries, both indirect — essayist E. B. White (born Elwyn Brooks White) and logician Haskell Curry (born Haskell Brooks Curry), neither of whom used Brooks as a given name.

That thin, middle-name-only namesake record, despite a data history running the full length of the dataset, mirrors Cooper's pattern from the fourth batch — a name whose recent popularity doesn't trace back to any individual actually called by it.

bryson.text: Bryson peaked on both measures in 2017 — 4,677 births, rank 86 — and has retreated 28% since, to 2,469 at rank 147. It belongs to the -son cohort with Jackson, Mason, Greyson and Dawson, and it is falling while Dawson is climbing, which is a useful caution against treating any of these sound-groups as moving in lockstep. Recorded from 1914, 81,069 births in total, essentially all since 1990. Two bearers are listed, both musicians: Bryson Tiller, born 1993, and the rapper Logic, whose given name is Sir Robert Bryson Hall. Neither predates the name's rise sufficiently to have caused it, which again points to pattern rather than person.

caleb.text:
Caleb's raw count peaked in 2002 at 11,665 births, but its rank kept climbing for another seven years, hitting #31 in 2009 — a longer lag than most names in this batch, similar in shape to Isaac's pattern from batch three.

By 2024 it had fallen to #49 with 5,766 births, down 38% from a decade before.

The enrichment data's oldest reference is the biblical spy Caleb, dated to roughly 1483 BC — one of the oldest specific dates attached to any name across all four batches so far — sitting alongside contemporary entries like actor Caleb McLaughlin and rapper Don Toliver, born Caleb Toliver.

callum.text: Callum is up 591% in ten years, the second-steepest climb here, and reached 2,258 births at rank 159 in 2024. Its cumulative total is only 13,076 — the smallest in this slice alongside Stetson — from a start in 1983. Every listed bearer is British and most are footballers: Callum Hudson-Odoi, born 2000, Callum Wilson, Callum McGregor, plus the actors Callum Turner and Callum Keith Rennie, born 1960. That concentration tells the story. Callum is a Scottish name that has been extremely popular in Britain since the 1990s and is only now crossing over, which puts it a full generation behind its usage elsewhere — a lag that is common with British imports and rarely noticed.

calvin.text: Calvin's best year on both measures was 1924 — 4,919 births, rank 44 — the year Calvin Coolidge, born 1872, won the presidency in his own right. A century later the name records 2,568 births at rank 140, and it is quietly up 10% over the decade, so this is stability rather than revival. Present since 1880 with 219,556 births logged. The bearer list is unusually good: Calvin Klein, born 1942, the Nobel laureate Edward Calvin Kendall, and two people known by other names entirely — Snoop Dogg, born Calvin Broadus, and Phil McGraw, whose first name is Phillip but who appears here regardless. Presidential names usually spike and collapse; Calvin spiked, collapsed and then found a floor, which is the rarer outcome.

cameron.text:
Cameron's count and rank peaked in the same year, 2000 — 12,765 births and #31 nationally — echoing the simultaneous-peak shape seen in Angel, Mila, and Isaiah elsewhere in this batch.

Since then it's fallen further than most: #66 by 2024, with 4,817 births, down 32% over the decade — a steeper decline than Josiah's or Charles's, closer to Ella's pace.

Cameron Diaz anchors the name in film, while voice actor Cam Clarke and rapper Wiz Khalifa (born Cameron Thomaz) round out a famous-bearer list that spans acting, animation, and music without concentrating in any single era.

camila.text:
Camila has held essentially the same rank, #11, since its 2020 peak — 8,164 births that year against 7,608 in 2024, a modest pullback in count but no real change in position, unlike several names in this batch whose rank has already dropped several places from its high point.

The name entered SSA records in 1914 and has grown 46% over the past decade, a steady climb rather than a sudden spike, with no gaps in its decades-active history since.

Its famous-bearer list is heavily contemporary and entertainment-driven — singer Camila Cabello, actor Camila Mendes, model Camila Morrone — almost entirely people born in the 1990s, a narrower generational cluster than names like Elias or John whose namesakes span centuries.

carlos.text: Carlos records 2,614 births at rank 135, a 24% ten-year decline against its 2001 high of 6,842 and a best rank of 59 in 1999. That decline is the mildest of the three Spanish staples in this batch — Luis is off 29%, Juan 33% — but the shape is identical, and 306,621 births since 1880 make it the deepest-rooted of them in American records. The file's headline bearer is Charles V, born 1500, listed under the English form of a monarch known in Spain as Carlos I; Charlie Sheen, born 1965, appears because he was born Carlos Estévez. Between an emperor filed under the wrong language and an actor who changed his name, this list needs more care than most before anything from it reaches a page.

caroline.text: Caroline reached rank 55 in 2017. Its busiest year for births was 2000, at 5,022 — seventeen years earlier, which is another case of a name climbing the table while producing fewer children. It now records 2,720 births at rank 92, down 37% across the decade. With 248,055 births since 1880 it is among the more established names here. The namesake list is almost entirely middle-name matches: Kirsten Dunst, Victoria Beckham and Gisele Bündchen all carry Caroline second, and none is known by it. The astronomer Caroline Herschel, born 1750, and the tennis player Caroline Wozniacki are the genuine bearers. A name this formal usually depends on a nickname to stay usable, and Caroline's supply of them is unusually deep.

carson.text: Carson's famous-bearer list is a good lesson in reading namesake data carefully. Macaulay Culkin appears because Carson is his middle name, and Carson McCullers was a woman who published under a name that now reads as overwhelmingly male. Neither is really a bearer in the sense a parent browsing this page would expect. The chart is more straightforward: a 2018 high of 5,259 births, then a slide to 2,890 by 2024, down 38% across the decade. Rank tells the same story, from 70 at that 2018 high to 123 now. Present in SSA records since 1880, Carson spent a century as a rare surname-style choice before the 1990s surname wave carried it up. Its all-time total of 137,777 is modest for a name with that much history, which confirms almost all of its volume is recent. What's fading now is the wave, not the name.

carter.text:
Carter's raw count peaked in 2015 at 10,814 and its rank peaked the same year at #24 — one of the rare cases in this batch where count and rank moved together instead of one lagging the other.

Since then it's dropped to #45, with 6,267 births in 2024 — 41% below its count a decade earlier, a steeper fall than Jackson's despite the earlier alignment between count and rank at the top.

Its famous-bearer list is thin and entirely contemporary — composer Carter Burwell, actor Carter Jenkins — with no historical figure predating the name's own rise, suggesting Carter's popularity was never really borrowed from an existing namesake the way Elizabeth's or Thomas's was.

charles.text:
Charles's best-ever rank, #4, was already set in 1880, the very first year this dataset covers — the same year Samuel, John, William, and Thomas each hit their own best-ever rank, a cluster of names whose positional peak arrived right at the start of what this dataset can track. The raw count didn't reach its own high, 40,779 births, until 1947, sixty-seven years later.

2,441,151 total births since 1880 makes Charles one of this batch's largest names by history. Its 2024 count, 5,593, sits 24% below where it was ten years back — a milder decline than Emily's or Abigail's despite the name's much longer run.

Charles Darwin, Charles Dickens, and King Charles III cover science, literature, and monarchy across three centuries, the kind of namesake breadth that only names with an 1880-era rank peak tend to carry.

charlie.text:
Charlie's rank hit its best mark absurdly early — #20 in 1881, just a year into this whole dataset — while the count itself didn't peak until 1919, at 2,891 births. That's 38 years between the two milestones.

Even with a 23% uptick over the past decade, Charlie now sits at #176 — the lowest current position of any name in this dataset, with just 2,084 births in 2024. Growth on paper doesn't always mean climbing the chart when the base is already this small.

Charlie Chaplin and jazz great Charlie Parker anchor the name's early-to-mid-century image; Charlie Puth and Charlie Hunnam carry it into the present.

charlotte.text:
Charlotte reached its highest-ever count in 2021 at 13,362 births and has eased only slightly since, to 12,552 in 2024 — a 24% rise over the decade despite dropping one rank position from its 2021 peak of #3 to #4 today, which points to a name holding steady while others around it move faster.

It's been in the SSA data continuously since 1880, but its modern rise is recent and sharp: the name spent most of the 20th century well below its current position before climbing through the 2010s. Princess Charlotte of Wales, born 2015, sits right at the start of that acceleration, though the name was already well into its ascent by then.

The literary association — Charlotte Brontë — gives the name a different kind of cultural weight than most current top-ten names carry, less tied to any specific celebrity generation and more to a centuries-old reference point, which may partly explain why its growth has been gradual rather than a sudden spike.

chloe.text:
Chloe's rank peaked at #9 in 2009, the same year its raw count hit its high of 11,918 births — one of this batch's cleaner simultaneous peaks, like Carter's or Mason's.

By 2024 its rank had drifted to #20 with 6,385 births, 25% under its count a decade back — a milder retreat than Jackson's or Gabriel's.

The enrichment data lists a single namesake, filmmaker Chloé Zhao, whose Oscar-winning career postdates the name's 2009 peak by more than a decade — meaning her prominence can't explain the name's original rise, only perhaps helping sustain interest in the years since.

christian.text:
Christian's biggest single year, 16,057 births, came in 2000; its best rank, #21, held six years later in 2006. From there the count fell 50% across the following decade, landing at 4,247 births in 2024, #77 nationally.

Every decade since 1880 shows up in this name's records, unusual staying power for one whose meaning ties directly to religious identity rather than a person.

Hans Christian Andersen anchors it in 19th-century Danish storytelling; Jodie Foster, born Alicia Christian Foster, carries it as a middle name into contemporary American film.

christopher.text:
Christopher's rank and count moved in opposite directions for over a decade: #2, the best rank, came first in 1972, while 60,019 births, the raw-count high, took until 1984 to arrive — a reversed version of the lag pattern seen in most other names, where count typically peaks before rank does.

Total US births run past two million for this name, and the 2024 count, 5,054, sits 51% below where it stood ten years earlier.

Johnny Depp (born John Christopher Depp), Chris Pratt, and Chris Pine keep the shortened form visible in contemporary film, while director Christopher Nolan carries the full name into a different corner of the same industry.

claire.text:
5,216 births and #40 nationally arrived together for Claire in 2016, its peak on both fronts. A 34% slide over the following decade brought it down to 3,329 births and #67 by 2024.

Since the dataset's opening in 1880, 210,623 babies have carried this name — a solid, unremarkable middle-of-the-pack total for this batch.

Nobel economist Elinor Ostrom's middle name was Claire; contemporary actors Claire Danes, Claire Holt, and Claire Foy span three separate generations of film, all born within a decade of each other.

clara.text: Two peaks, thirty-three years apart, and they mean different things. Clara's rank high of 7 came in 1885, when a handful of names covered most of the field. Its raw birth high of 5,778 arrived in 1918, by which point it had already slipped down the rankings. That gap is the clearest illustration on this site of why rank and count are not interchangeable measures. What makes Clara unusual today is direction: up 7% over the past decade, to 3,060 births and rank 78, while most names of similar vintage keep sliding. It has appeared in every decade since 1880 and carries an all-time total of 297,914. The namesakes skew European and pre-war — Clara Schumann, born 1819, Clara Zetkin, Clara Bow — which suits a name that reads as recovered rather than invented.

colton.text:
Colton peaked twice, years apart: 6,488 births in 2013 by raw count, #59 by rank six years later in 2019. The 44% decline since brought it to 3,588 births and #98 in 2024.

This name's own records start in 1913, more than three decades into the dataset, and total US births reach 148,712 over that span.

Reality TV and film actor Colton Haynes is the only namesake the enrichment data offers — a single contemporary figure for a name whose popularity has already peaked and turned.

connor.text: Connor is down 64% across the decade, the second-sharpest decline in this batch behind Blake. It peaked hard and specifically: 10,049 births in 2004 at rank 38, the highest single-year count of any name in this slice, now reduced to 2,606 at rank 136. First recorded in 1913, with 234,024 births almost entirely accumulated between 1990 and 2010. No origin is listed, and the bearers are all athletes born in the 1990s — Connor McDavid, born 1997, Connor Wickham, Connor Roberts — which is to say they are the generation the name produced rather than the reason for it. A name that concentrated inside two decades becomes a reliable age marker, and that is precisely what makes it hard to choose now.

cooper.text:
Cooper's 2024 count, 5,699 births, is a fresh high on both fronts — its best-ever rank, #50, arrived the same year. An 18% climb over the past decade is modest compared to several other risers in this batch, but it's been a steady one rather than a sudden spike.

The name has technically been in the data since 1882, though its enrichment list carries only one entry: footballer Glen Johnson, whose middle name is Cooper — an indirect connection rather than someone actually named Cooper at birth.

That thin namesake record, despite a data history stretching back well over a century, suggests Cooper functioned mostly as a surname-turned-first-name until quite recently, without a strong individual figure driving its adoption.

cora.text: Cora ranked 15 in 1880, in the first year the SSA counted anything, which places it among the genuinely Victorian names on this site. Its highest birth count came 139 years later, in 2019, at 3,601 — the sort of gap that only appears when a name dies out completely and returns. Currently 2,570 births at rank 102, off 13% from that recent high, with 153,964 births accumulated. Only one bearer is recorded, and indirectly: Koko Taylor, born 1928, the blues singer, whose given name was Cora Walton. For a name with this much history that is a remarkably thin file, and it is characteristic of Victorian revivals generally — the people who carried them originally were rarely famous, and the people carrying them now are children.

daisy.text:
1880 produced Daisy's best-ever rank, #48 — right alongside Arthur, elsewhere in this batch, whose own positional peak also landed in the dataset's opening year. The raw count set a separate record much later, 2024: 3,091 births, up 73% from a decade before.

This name's grand total sits at 156,125 births since 1880, a solid middle-of-the-pack figure for this batch.

Star Wars's Daisy Ridley and Normal People's Daisy Edgar-Jones keep it current on screen, alongside two fictional entries — Donald Duck's Daisy Duck and Nintendo's Princess Daisy.

damian.text:
3,974 births, #98 nationally — that's Damian's 2013 peak on both measures. A milder-than-most 17% decline followed over the next decade, to 3,233 births and #110 by 2024.

Damian only enters the data in 1912, later than most of this dataset's established names, and total US births now stand at 107,019.

NBA All-Star Damian Lillard and reggae musician Damian Marley, Bob Marley's youngest son, keep the name current across sport and music; decathlete Damian Warner adds a third field entirely, track and field.

daniel.text:
Daniel peaked in 1985 at 38,564 births — more than four times its current count — and the name has been declining steadily since, down 40% over just the past decade to 8,391 in 2024, the second-steepest ten-year percentage drop in this batch, behind only Ava's 45%.

It's been recorded since 1880 and has held a top-20 rank continuously for most of the past several decades, meaning its current #16 position, while down from a 1985 rank of #5, still represents remarkable staying power for a name this far past its peak.

Its famous-bearer list spans jazz (Louis Armstrong, whose middle name was Daniel), literature (Daniel Defoe), and film (Daniel Radcliffe, Daniel Craig) — a name that has apparently supplied recognizable public figures in every generation since the 1900s without needing a fresh cultural spike to stay in circulation, even as its raw birth numbers fall.

david.text:
David's scale places it among the largest names in this entire dataset: 3,682,683 total US births since 1880, with a single-year peak of 86,301 in 1955. Its best-ever rank, #1, came five years later in 1960 — the same lagged pattern seen in Ethan and Dylan, where a name's positional peak trails its raw-count peak.

By 2024 its rank had dropped to #31, with 7,317 births — 40% below where it stood a decade earlier, a steeper decline than John's or Samuel's despite a broadly similar historical arc.

Its famous-bearer list spans philosophy (David Hume), mathematics (David Hilbert), and politics (David Cameron, Dwight D. Eisenhower's full name includes David) across four centuries, a breadth that puts it in the same historical tier as John or Michael even though its current rank sits noticeably lower than either.

dawson.text: Dawson's highest birth count came in 1999, at 2,802, which places it squarely inside the run of Dawson's Creek. The interesting part is what has happened since: after falling away for two decades, the name is up 138% over the past ten years, to 2,576 births at rank 139. That is a second wave, and second waves are rare — most television-driven names never recover once the show ends. First recorded in 1885 with 51,610 births logged. The two listed bearers, the actor Richard Kiel, born 1939, and the guitarist Johnny Winter, are both middle-name matches and neither has any bearing on either peak. What is lifting it now is the -son ending shared with Jackson, Mason and Greyson, not the show.

dean.text: Dean's highest birth count came in 1961 and its best rank in 1967, both squarely in the Dean Martin era — Martin was born in 1917 and at his most visible through those years. What is more interesting is the present: up 49% over the decade to 2,545 births at rank 142, making this a genuine second act rather than a long fade. With 192,948 births since 1880 there is plenty of history to revive. The file lists Dean Acheson, born 1893, alongside three actors who carry it in the middle — Harry Dean Stanton, Richard Dean Anderson and the astronaut Edgar Mitchell. Single-syllable midcentury boys' names have come back as a group, and Dean has moved further than most of them.

declan.text: Declan peaked in 2019 at 3,971 births and rank 95, and has given back 17% over the decade to reach 2,758 and rank 131. Few names here have both risen and fallen this completely within living memory — nothing before 1951, and 56,351 births in total across that short span. The Irish saint the name derives from is absent from the file; the two listed bearers, the footballer Declan Rice, born 1999, and the singer Declan Galbraith, born 1991, are both younger than the name's American revival. Irish imports as a category have cooled after a long run, and Declan looks like a name that arrived with that wave and is now easing back down with it.

delilah.text:
4,240 births and #50 nationally — both fresh territory for Delilah in 2024, up 69% from ten years before.

Only one figure appears in the enrichment data: the biblical Delilah, dated to roughly 1100 BC — younger than Leah's and Hannah's biblical references elsewhere in this batch, but older than Ezekiel's 620 BC and Isaiah's 765 BC from the fourth batch.

Nothing else shows up at all — an unusually singular, ancient anchor with no modern namesake pulling in the same direction.

diego.text: Diego records 2,506 births at rank 145, having come off a 2006 peak where it hit 8,403 births and rank 56 simultaneously. The 21% decline since is the gentlest of any Spanish-origin name across these four batches. Recorded from 1887, absent only in the 1890s, and 124,028 births deep. The bearer list is genuinely outstanding — Diego Velázquez, born 1599, Diego Rivera, born 1886, and Diego Maradona, born 1960 — and contains one clear error: Diego Forlán, born 1979, is filed as a tennis player when he is a footballer, and a well-known one. Errors of that kind are worth catching before anything from these lists reaches a page, because they are invisible unless you already know the person.

dominic.text:
6,335 births, #68 nationally — Dominic's high point on both fronts, set in 2013. From there, a 47% retreat over ten years brought it to 3,290 births and #108 by 2024.

Records for this name begin just five years into the dataset, back in 1885; 191,358 births have been recorded under it since.

Lost's Dominic Monaghan, philosopher Ivan Illich, and UK minister Dominic Raab have essentially nothing in common besides sharing this name across three completely unrelated fields of work.

dylan.text:
Dylan is one of the youngest names in this batch by data history: it first appears in US birth records only in 1953, decades later than the 1880 starting point most names in this range share. Its count peaked in 2001 at 16,497, but its best-ever rank, #19, wasn't reached until 2003 — the same lagged pattern seen in Ethan.

By 2024 its rank had slipped to #28, with 7,464 births — 28% below where it stood a decade earlier, a milder decline than Ethan's or Michael's but still a clear retreat from its early-2000s high.

Its famous-bearer list skews almost entirely toward film and streaming — Dylan O'Brien, Dylan Minnette, Jack Dylan Grazer — young actors rather than an older cultural reference, consistent with a name whose entire US popularity has unfolded within living memory rather than across generations.

easton.text:
Easton's count and rank both crested in 2016 — 5,642 births, #66 nationally — before a 33% pullback over the following ten years left it at 3,336 births and #103 by 2024, out of 77,195 total US births carried by this name since 1907.

Records for this name begin in 1907, missing the dataset's first quarter-century.

Photographer Ansel Adams, whose middle name was Easton, is the enrichment data's only bearer — an indirect namesake for a name whose actual popularity arrived a century after his birth.

eden.text:
Both of Eden's measures hit new territory in 2024 at once, 3,115 births and #72 nationally, 46% ahead of where the name stood ten years back.

This one skipped the dataset's early decades entirely — nothing on record before 1943, more recent than most names covered so far.

Belgian footballer Eden Hazard and Israel's 2024 Eurovision entrant Eden Golan give the name real international visibility, alongside American rapper CupcakKe, born Elizabeth Harris, who performs under a stage name that has nothing to do with it.

eleanor.text:
Eleanor's raw count actually peaked back in 1920 at 8,497 births. A 91% climb over the last ten years — among the larger gains in this batch — still hasn't been enough to push 2024's count of 7,127 past that century-old high. It's a similar shape to Evelyn's story in the top-25 batch: an early-20th-century peak, a long quiet stretch, and a modern recovery that's real but not yet complete.

Its rank, unlike its count, has already reached a new high — #14 in 2023 — since the smaller pool of competing names today means fewer births are needed to hold a strong position than in 1920.

The famous-bearer list carries unusual political and literary weight: Eleanor Roosevelt, Margaret Atwood (born Margaret Eleanor Atwood), and medieval queen Eleanor of Aquitaine span eight centuries, a range matched by few other names in this batch.

elena.text:
Elena's 2024 count, 4,567 births, and its best-ever rank, #45, arrived together — 75% above its count from ten years before.

This name's SSA data goes back to 1880, a long, quiet history before this recent acceleration.

Its famous-bearer list is unusually political and international — Romanian dictator's wife Elena Ceaușescu, Rome's former mayor Virginia Raggi (whose middle name is Elena), and cosmonaut-adjacent Bulgarian singer Inna (born Elena Alexandra Apostoleanu) — a spread across Eastern Europe that doesn't resemble the largely American or British namesake lists common elsewhere in this batch.

eli.text:
Half its 2012 self, roughly — Eli's 2024 count of 3,723 is down 50% from its count a decade prior, one of the sharper falls in this batch. That 2012 peak, 8,076 births, also marked the rank's own high point, #43, both landing the same year.

Records for this name go back to the dataset's start in 1880.

Eli Whitney's cotton gin ties the name to early American industry; scholar Ibn Hazm, born the year 994, is by far the oldest figure linked to any name covered in this batch, predating even Amir's medieval namesakes.

eliana.text:
Eliana's 2024 figures are records on both counts: 6,423 births, #18 nationally, 134% higher than its count from ten years back — one of this batch's biggest percentage gains, trailing only Maverick and Aurora.

Unlike most names in this range, it doesn't trace back to 1880: the earliest recorded year is 1961, and the name barely registered until recent decades, making its current size almost entirely a product of growth within the last twenty years.

The enrichment data has no famous bearers listed at all, the same gap seen with Aurora — two of this batch's fastest-growing names have essentially no documented namesake pulling their popularity, which suggests whatever is driving their rise isn't showing up as a single traceable cultural reference.

elias.text:
Elias is still climbing without any sign of a turn: both its count and its rank hit new highs in the same year, 2024 — 7,653 births at #25 nationally, 102% higher than a decade earlier. Unlike Leo or Owen, whose rank has already started pulling back from a recent peak, Elias hasn't yet shown that kind of reversal.

SSA records go back to 1880 for this name, more than a century of quiet background presence before this recent acceleration.

Its famous-bearer list is unusually cross-disciplinary for a name this size — Walt Disney (born Walter Elias Disney), Nobel-winning writer Elias Canetti, 12th-century Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi (born Elyas), and Brazilian former president Michel Temer (born Michel Miguel Elias Temer Lulia) — a spread across entertainment, literature, poetry, and politics that most similarly-sized names don't match.

elijah.text:
Elijah peaked in 2011 at 13,997 births and has fallen 20% over the past decade to 11,171 in 2024, dropping from its best-ever rank of #4 in 2020 to #8 today — a decline that's milder than Sophia's or Isabella's but points the same direction: biblical names that surged in the 2000s and 2010s cooling from their highs.

The name has been in continuous SSA use since 1880, giving it well over a century of quiet presence before its 21st-century rise, similar to Noah's pattern but on a smaller scale and with an earlier peak.

Its famous-bearer list is notably eclectic for a biblical name — actor Elijah Wood, musician Lil Peep, Nation of Islam leader Elijah Muhammad, Olympic swimmer Elijah Winnington — spanning very different public identities rather than reinforcing one image, which may be part of why the name reads as flexible rather than tied to any single association.

eliza.text: Eliza ranked 85 in 1880 and did not reach its highest birth count until 2021 — 141 years apart, the widest such gap in this batch. It has grown 44% across the decade to 2,303 births at rank 118, so the revival is ongoing rather than finished. Cumulative total 68,370. The bearers are heavily nineteenth-century and heavily indirect: Frances Hodgson Burnett, born 1849, and Gene Tierney, born 1920, both carried Eliza second; Elisa Bonaparte, born 1777, is spelled differently; Eliza McCardle Johnson, born 1810, was a First Lady. Hamilton, which put an Eliza centre stage from 2015, is nowhere in the file despite lining up neatly with the curve.

elizabeth.text:
Elizabeth carries the widest gap in this batch between its rank peak and its count peak: the rank hit #3, its best ever, in 1887 — seven years into the dataset — while the raw count didn't peak until 1990, when a single year brought 20,749 births — a 103-year gap between the two milestones.

Total births run to 1,687,089 since 1880, and the 2024 figure of 6,878 marks a 28% decline from ten years earlier, landing at #17.

Two English queens (Elizabeth I, Elizabeth II) sit alongside poet Emily Dickinson and actress Elizabeth Taylor on the famous-bearer list — a name whose royal association predates its American popularity by centuries, unlike most names in this batch whose namesakes are contemporaries of the parents choosing them.

ella.text:
346,302 total births puts Ella well ahead of most names in this batch by scale, though still a fraction of the oldest, largest names here like Charles's 2.4 million. Its count peaked in 2010 at 9,883, and the rank followed a year later at #12 in 2011.

The decline since has been substantial: 5,685 births in 2024, 34% fewer than ten years before, at #30 nationally.

Ella Fitzgerald anchors the name in mid-20th-century jazz, while Lorde (born Ella Yelich-O'Connor) and actor Ella Purnell keep it current — a spread from the 1930s through the 2020s that gives the name unusual reach for one that's fallen this far from its peak.

ellie.text:
Ellie's count and rank both reached fresh peaks in 2024: 6,306 births, #21 nationally, 41% higher than its count from a decade back — a steadier climb than the triple-digit gains posted by Maverick, Aurora, or Eliana.

The name has been present since 1880, though its enrichment data suggests it functions largely as a short form: actor Ellie Kemper and singer Blanche (born Ellie Delvaux) are its only listed namesakes, both relatively recent.

That shortage of older reference points, paired with a century-plus data history, suggests Ellie has spent most of its recorded existence as an informal nickname rather than a name chosen outright at birth — only recently becoming common enough as a given name to show up this prominently on its own.

elliot.text: Elliot, single T, hit records on both measures in 2022 and now records 2,370 births at rank 150, up 34% over ten years. It runs about a hundred and fifty places ahead of its two-T twin while growing slightly slower, so the gap between the spellings is narrowing. Present since 1880, 62,934 births total. Elliot Page, born 1987, is the most prominent current bearer; Alex Salmond, born 1954, and the internet pioneer Bob Kahn carry it as a middle name. Having both spellings land inside a single twenty-five-name slice is the clearest possible demonstration of a problem that runs through this whole dataset: SSA counts strings, not names, and parents choosing between Elliot and Elliott are choosing the same name twice.

elliott.text: The two-T spelling is the less common of the pair, and it is the one growing faster: up 39% over the decade against Elliot's 34%. Elliott records 2,219 births at rank 163, its best count arriving in 2019 and best rank in 2020. Together the spellings would place considerably higher than either does alone, which is the same measurement problem Madeline has. Present since 1880 with 67,925 births logged. The bearers split neatly by field — Elliott Smith, born 1969, Elliott Gould, the photographer Elliott Erwitt and the composer Elliott Carter — while Pierre Trudeau, born 1919, appears on a middle name. Two entries in this batch differing only by a consonant is itself evidence of how fragmented modern naming has become.

eloise.text:
217% growth over the past decade — the second-largest gain in this batch behind only Atlas and Luka — brought Eloise to a fresh 2024 high: 3,430 births, #64 nationally.

The name's own records run the full length of this dataset, from 1880 on, mostly quiet until this recent climb.

The enrichment data offers no namesake at all, leaving one of this batch's bigger risers without a single traceable cultural anchor — the same gap seen with Atlas and Paisley elsewhere in this range.

emerson.text:
#270 nationally with 1,270 births — Emerson trails almost everything else in this batch by current standing, though it's actually down only slightly from a 2019 peak of 1,343, when the rank also hit its own best, #268, a year later.

Every single decade since 1880 shows at least some record of this name, and its total, 63,935 births, reflects that long, quiet consistency.

Astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard and racing champion Emerson Fittipaldi anchor it in science and motorsport, an unusually low-key namesake pair.

emery.text:
56% growth across the last ten years brought Emery to 3,197 births in 2024, though the rank's own best, #70, actually arrived a year earlier, in 2023 — an unusual case of rank leading rather than trailing the count.

This name's history starts in 1906, missing the dataset's first quarter-century entirely.

Just one namesake is listed in the enrichment data: Olympic sprinter Mel Patton, whose middle name was Emery — an indirect connection for a name whose recent rise has no other documented reference point.

emilia.text:
Emilia's 4,634 births in 2024 sits 131% higher than its count from ten years back, though it trails the name's actual peak, 4,851 in 2021 — the year count and rank both set their high points together, #40 nationally.

SSA records for this name run back to 1880, a quiet background presence for most of that span before this recent surge.

Emilia Clarke's television fame, beginning in 2011, sits right at the start of the name's climb — one of the clearer possible cultural connections in this batch, though the birth data can only show the timing lines up, not that it caused the rise.

emiliano.text:
111% growth across the past decade put Emiliano at a fresh 2024 record for both count and rank together: 3,125 births, #113 nationally.

There's a real hole in this name's history — first appearing in 1885, then absent through the 1890s and 1900s specifically, before returning in the 1910s and continuing steadily since.

Revolutionary leader Emiliano Zapata anchors it in early-1900s Mexican history; a cluster of contemporary footballers, all born in the 1980s and 1990s, keeps it visible on the pitch today.

emilio.text: Emilio set records on both measures in 2024, at 2,358 births and rank 152, capping 84% growth across the decade. Recorded from 1882 but only 51,599 births deep, so almost all of its American volume is recent. The bearer list spans an unusual range: the physicist Emilio Segrè, born 1905, a Nobel laureate; Emilio Aguinaldo, born 1869, the first president of the Philippines; Emilio Estevez, born 1962. Clement X, born 1590, was Emilio Altieri before his papal name, and Mwai Kibaki, president of Kenya, carried Emilio first. This is the same Italian and Spanish broadening that has lifted Lorenzo, Matteo and Lucia, and Emilio is moving at roughly the same speed as those.

emily.text:
892,769 total US births make Emily one of the largest names in this dataset, on par with Joseph or Matthew from earlier batches. It was the #1 girls' name for a long run through the late 1990s, its rank peaking in 1996 and its raw count peaking three years later at 26,542 births in 1999.

The fall since has been steep: 5,955 births in 2024, 53% under its count from ten years earlier, landing at #25 — a sharper drop than most names that once held the top spot.

Emily Dickinson and Emily Brontë give the name serious 19th-century literary weight, while Emily Blunt keeps it current — a spread across two centuries that few names still in the top 30 can claim.

emma.text:
Emma is the clearest case among the current top names of a peak already passed: it topped the chart at 22,719 births in 2003 and held #1 through 2008, but 2024's count of 13,485 is down 36% from a decade ago, even though it still ranks #2 nationally.

That gap between rank and raw count is the real story here. Emma's own numbers make the point: it needed 22,719 births to be the #1 name in 2003, but today's #2 spot only takes 13,485, well under two-thirds of that — because parents are drawing from a much wider pool of choices than they were twenty years ago. Emma isn't fading so much as the whole naming landscape has spread out underneath it.

The name has been recorded every year since 1880, and its famous bearers — Jane Austen's Emma predates the data, but Emma Watson, Emma Thompson, and Emma Goldman span acting and activism across more than a century — suggest a name that's been quietly available the whole time, waiting for its turn rather than arriving with any single moment.

emmett.text: Emmett carries more historical weight than its numbers suggest. Emmett Till, born 1941, is the name's most significant bearer by a wide margin, and his murder in 1955 is a fixed point in American civil rights history. Any account of this name that treats it as a light vintage revival is incomplete. The chart itself is unremarkable in a good way: a 2021 high of 3,662 births easing to 3,001, rank 119 against a best of 103, and a decade trend still positive at 14%. It has been present since 1880 without ever becoming common, which is why the all-time total sits at just 75,881. Van Heflin, born 1908, appears via his given name Emmett. This is a name with deep roots and modest usage — an unusual combination in a batch full of recent coinages.

enzo.text:
Enzo's 435% growth over the past decade ranks second-largest in this batch, behind only Lainey's 901%, with 4,548 births and #74 nationally both marking fresh highs in 2024.

SSA records for this name start in 1915, though its decades-active list skips the 1940s entirely — a full decade with fewer than five recorded births — before resuming and eventually climbing sharply in the 2020s.

The namesake list here leans football, much like Thiago's in the fourth batch, though Enzo's cluster centers on Enzo Ferrari's automotive legacy at one end and contemporary players like Enzo Fernández at the other, a wider span of fields than Thiago's all-footballer list.

ethan.text:
Ethan shows a pattern worth flagging because it recurs across several names in this range: its raw count peaked in 2004 at 22,210 births, but its best-ever rank, #2, didn't arrive until 2009 — five years after the count itself started falling. A name's rank can keep climbing even as its own numbers shrink, if its competitors are shrinking faster.

By 2024 that rank has slid to #19, with 8,170 births, down 48% from a decade earlier — one of the steeper ten-year declines among boys' names in this range, alongside Michael's.

Its famous-bearer list skews almost entirely contemporary, tilted toward European football (Ethan Ampadu, Ethan Nwaneri) and American film (Ethan Hawke, Ethan Suplee), a spread that contrasts with older names like Samuel or Michael whose namesakes reach back centuries — reflecting how recently Ethan actually built its popularity, first entering the data only in 1882.

eva.text: Eva ranked 31 in 1889. Its busiest year for births came in 1918, at 4,563, after which it spent most of the twentieth century declining before a partial recovery. It is currently down 38% across the decade, at 2,296 births and rank 120, with 283,587 births accumulated since 1880. The bearers are a genuinely uncomfortable mix: Eva Perón, born 1919, Eva Braun, born 1912, Eva Green and Eva Longoria, with Hedy Lamarr, born 1914, appearing under her birth name Hedwig Eva Kiesler. Few short names carry associations pulling in such opposite directions. Eva's brevity and cross-language portability — it works unchanged in a dozen European languages — are what have kept it in continuous use regardless.

evan.text: Evan has shed 62% in ten years, dropping from 10,295 births in 2007 and rank 35 in 2009 to 2,526 at rank 143. Its 289,934 births are packed almost entirely into the thirty years around that peak, which is why the name now carries such a precise generational signal. Of Welsh origin, recorded from 1880. Van Heflin turns up in the bearer file again here, as he does under Emmett — the actor was christened Emmett Evan Heflin, so he legitimately belongs to both, which is a useful reminder that a single person can inflate several of these lists at once. Evan Peters, born 1987, and the basketball player Evan Fournier are the genuine modern bearers. Ben Miller, born 1966, is another middle-name match.

evelyn.text:
Evelyn's story runs opposite to most names in this batch: it actually peaked back in 1921 at 14,278 births, decades before almost every other name here reached its high point, and has spent the century since well below that level — its 2024 count of 9,116 is still 4% higher than a decade ago, a slow modern recovery rather than a decline from a recent peak.

The name has been recorded every year since 1880, giving it one of the longest and most stable histories in this batch, present through the entire 20th century rather than arriving as a recent addition like Mateo or Ezra.

Its famous-bearer list spans writer Evelyn Waugh, ballerina Margot Fonteyn, and actress Angela Bassett — a name used by both men and women historically (Waugh was male), which may partly explain its unusually long, low-drama presence in the data rather than the sharp peak-and-decline pattern more common among names tied to one specific era or gender association.

everett.text:
#81 in 1906 was Everett's earliest rank peak; the count didn't catch up until 2021, at 4,250 births — 115 years apart, one of the widest gaps seen anywhere in this dataset, trailing only Samuel's 121 years and Grace's 120.

56% growth over the past decade brought the name to 3,947 births in 2024, at #85 nationally.

Painter John Everett Millais and Civil War general Ambrose Burnside, who carried Everett as a middle name, anchor it in 19th-century art and military history — far older than its recent popularity would suggest.

everly.text: The gaps in Everly's record are the interesting part. It first appears in 1944, then shows up only in the 1960s, 1980s and 1990s before becoming continuous — decades of complete absence from SSA data in between. Very few names in this batch have a history that broken. The modern run has been steep: a 2019 high of 4,780 births at rank 42, settling to 3,008 and rank 81, with a decade trend still up 61%. No famous bearers are recorded at all, which for a name this popular is unusual, though the Everly Brothers are the obvious unlisted association. An all-time total of 40,697 against that recent volume means the overwhelming majority of everyone ever named Everly is currently a child.

ezekiel.text:
Ezekiel's 5,390 births in 2024 is 126% above its count a decade prior, with both its count and rank peaking together two years earlier, in 2022, at #48 nationally.

The enrichment data's oldest reference dates to roughly 620 BC — the biblical prophet — making Ezekiel one of three names in this batch, alongside Caleb and Isaiah, whose famous-bearer list reaches back into antiquity via a biblical figure with a negative birth year on record.

Its more recent namesakes are almost entirely athletic — steeplechase runner Ezekiel Kemboi, bodybuilder Ezekiel Jackson — a contrast between an ancient religious origin and a thoroughly modern set of contemporary bearers.

ezra.text:
Ezra had its single best year on record in 2024, with 8,774 births — its current count and its all-time peak are the same number, meaning the name hasn't yet shown any sign of slowing. The 156% rise over the past decade is the third-largest ten-year gain in this batch, behind only Theodore and Mateo.

It's been present in SSA data since 1880 but, like Mateo, stayed a minor presence for most of that span; nearly all of its current volume reflects growth within the last fifteen years, making it one of the more recently arrived names in the current top 15 by historical weight.

The famous-bearer list mixes the biblical scribe Ezra with poet Ezra Pound and actor Ezra Miller, plus musician George Ezra, whose stage name uses it as a surname rather than a given name — a reminder that a name's public visibility doesn't always come from people who were given it at birth.

gabriel.text:
Gabriel reached its best-ever rank, #21, in 2010, two years on from the birth-count peak of 13,040 in 2008 — a short lag similar to Isaac's.

Since then it's slid to #43, with 6,379 births in 2024 — 42% fewer than a decade earlier, a decline close to Jackson's in scale.

The famous-bearer list is unusually varied in tone — novelist Jules Verne, dictator Robert Mugabe, gangster Al Capone, physicist Gabriel Lippmann, and Chile's president Gabriel Boric — spanning fiction, politics, crime, and science in a way that doesn't cluster around any single kind of public figure the way Carter's or Maverick's shorter, more contemporary lists do.

gabriella.text: Gabriella peaked in 2009 and 2010 on rank and count respectively, reaching 33 and 6,183 births, and has since fallen 51% to 2,496 at rank 106.
