The timing sits neatly alongside a run of High School Musical films whose lead character carried the name, though the file records none of that. What it does record is Princess Gabriella of Monaco, born 2014, too late to matter, and H.E.R., born 1997, whose given name is Gabriella Wilson. Present since 1890 with 135,122 births. Its longer sibling Gabrielle and its shorter one Gabby split the same territory, so this is another entry where the counted string understates how many children answer to some version of it.

gael.text:
3,855 births and a fresh best-ever rank, #89 — both landed for Gael in 2024, up 113% from a decade earlier.

This name's history has a real hole in it: first recorded in 1919, then absent through the 1960s and 1970s specifically, before resuming in the 1980s and climbing steadily since.

Nearly every namesake here plays professional sport under the accented spelling Gaël — Clichy, Monfils, Kakuta — a tight cluster of contemporary French footballers and one tennis player, nothing older.

genesis.text:
4,351 births was Genesis's count high, set in 2016; its rank had already peaked three years earlier, at #55 in 2013. The slide since has been mild — just 8% in the past ten years, landing at 3,835 births in 2024.

Records here start comparatively late, 1964, and only one namesake shows up: industrial musician Genesis P-Orridge, active from the 1970s.

A recent data start, a single unconventional namesake, and a name pulled straight from religious text rather than a person — that combination sets Genesis apart from this batch's other biblical entries, Hannah and Delilah, whose oldest references are actual figures rather than a book title.

george.text: At 1,494,369 births all time, George is the largest name here by an enormous distance — more than fourteen hundred thousand American boys, and roughly seven times Madeline's total. It ranked 4 in 1881 and peaked at 27,476 births in 1921. Today it records 2,890 at rank 124, yet the ten-year change is only −4%, which makes it simultaneously the most fallen and the most currently stable name here. It has bottomed out. The bearers are as heavyweight as any list on the site: George Washington, born 1732, Lord Byron, born 1788, George Orwell, born 1903, and two presidents named Bush. A name can be this historically saturated and still sit outside the top hundred, which says more about how naming has fragmented than about George.

georgia.text: Georgia has almost exactly recovered a peak set in 1947. Its highest birth count was 2,475 that year; it currently records 2,458, having grown 84% across the decade. That is about as close to a full round trip as this dataset produces, and it puts Georgia alongside Leon as a name that has genuinely returned rather than merely stopped falling. Rank is another matter — 81 back in 1882 against 110 now — because the field has widened so much. Present since 1880 with 164,380 births. Only two bearers are listed, the actor Georgia Engel, born 1948, and the footballer Georgia Stanway, which is thin for a name that doubles as a US state and a country.

gianna.text:
Gianna's 98% gain over the past decade ranks among this batch's bigger percentage climbs, though its rank actually peaked earlier than its most recent high — #13 in 2020, the same year as its raw-count peak of 7,899 — and has eased slightly since to #23 with 6,097 births in 2024.

The name entered SSA data in 1951, later than most of this batch's older entries but earlier than recent arrivals like Maverick or Aiden.

Its enrichment data lists musician Gianna Nannini as the clearer namesake, an Italian recording artist active since the 1970s — consistent with the name's Italian origin, similar to how Santiago's and Camila's famous-bearer lists in the second batch skewed toward their own linguistic roots.

giovanni.text: The namesakes here span nearly seven hundred years: Boccaccio, born 1313, the composer Palestrina, born 1525, and Guglielmo Marconi, born 1874, who carried Giovanni among his given names. Francis of Assisi, born 1182, was christened Giovanni before the name he is known by. Against that, the American data is brief — nothing before 1907, and just 87,354 births in total. Current figures show 2,951 births at rank 122, down 9% over the decade from a 2010 high of 3,434. That mild decline puts it among the more stable names in this batch. Giovanni's American usage has always been tied to Italian-American families rather than to broad adoption, and unlike Lorenzo, which is climbing hard, it has stayed roughly where it settled.

grace.text:
Grace's rank peaked in 1883, just three years into this dataset, while 12,781 births — the raw-count high — didn't show up until 2003, a 120-year gap between the two milestones — one of the widest gaps observed across every batch so far, second only to Samuel's 121-year gap from the second batch.

531,126 total births since 1880 make it one of the larger names in this range, and the 2024 count, 5,002, is down 35% from a decade earlier.

Grace Kelly and computing pioneer Grace Hopper anchor the name across mid-century film and science, while Chloë Grace Moretz carries it into the present as a middle name rather than a given one.

graham.text: Graham is at its high point right now: 2,789 births in 2024, rank 129, both bests. Growth of 37% over ten years, from a base first recorded in 1881. The namesake list leans on middle names more than it looks — Alexander Graham Bell, born 1847, carried it second, as did David Niven and Terry Jones. Graham Greene, born 1904, is the clearest case of someone actually known by it. What the numbers show is a name that spent well over a century as a low-frequency British import and only recently found American traction; 58,681 births across that entire span is very little for a name present since the 1880s. It has no strong generational stamp, which is unusual and probably the point for parents choosing it.

grayson.text:
Grayson is one of the more stable names in this batch: 6,211 births in 2024 is down just 6% from a decade earlier, a far milder move than the double-digit swings affecting most of its neighbors here.

It entered SSA data later than most, in 1905. Its best rank, #32, arrived in 2018, a year past the birth-count high of 8,717 set in 2017 — one of the shorter lags in this batch.

The enrichment data has nothing to offer for famous bearers, the third name in this batch (with Aurora and Eliana) whose recent popularity isn't attached to any documented namesake at all — a pattern that seems to cluster specifically among this batch's newer, sound-driven names rather than its historically rooted ones.

greyson.text: Greyson's real problem is that half its bearers are spelled Grayson. The two variants split a single sound between them, so both charts understate how often the name is actually heard. This spelling first appears in 1965, peaked at 4,848 births in 2017 with a best rank of 77 the following year, and now records 2,868 at rank 127, down 6% over ten years. The all-time total of 58,563 covers barely sixty years. The one recorded namesake, the musician Greyson Chance, born 1997, went viral in 2010, which is close enough to the rise to be suggestive without being convincing on its own. Colour names for boys have had a strong run, but the -son ending that carried Jackson and Mason is the more likely engine here.

hadley.text: Hadley is off 21% from a 2014 peak that set both its records at once, 3,015 births and rank 100, and now records 2,380 at rank 114. Recorded from 1964, 46,412 births in total, no listed origin and no bearers at all. Hadley Richardson, the first wife of Ernest Hemingway, is the association most often cited for this name and is not in the file. Structurally it is a surname with a -ley ending, which places it with Kinsley and Everly, and all three have now either peaked or flattened. That cohort rose together through the 2010s and appears to be topping out together, which is what usually happens to names carried by a suffix rather than a meaning.

hailey.text: Hailey climbed to rank 19 in 2010. The most births it ever recorded, 8,798, had come seven years before that, in 2003 — top-twenty placement on materially fewer births than it had managed at the start of the decade. It has since fallen 43%, to 2,620 births and rank 100. Recorded from 1963 with 179,122 births, essentially all after 1990. The single listed bearer is Hailey Bieber, born 1996, who is younger than the name's rise and cannot account for it. Haley, Hayley, Haleigh and Hailee split the same sound between them, so this is another entry where the spelling shown captures only a fraction of the children actually answering to it.

hannah.text:
23,087 births in 2000 was Hannah's raw-count peak; the rank had already hit its own best, #2, two years earlier in 1998 — a genuine near-#1 run. From there: a 39% fall over the past decade, down to 4,054 births and #52 in 2024.

The enrichment data's oldest reference dates to roughly 1200 BC, the biblical mother of Samuel — older than Delilah's 1100 BC reference in this same batch, though younger than Leah's 1730 BC, also in this batch, and Jacob's 1790 BC from the third batch.

Hannah Arendt lends the name real philosophical weight; actor Hannah Murray keeps it visible on screen today.

harper.text:
Harper is one of the youngest names in this entire batch by history: it first appears in SSA data only in 1971, more than a century after most of its neighbors here, and its enrichment data lists exactly one famous bearer — novelist Harper Lee, born Nelle Harper Lee in 1926, whose fame predates the name's use as a first name by decades.

Its rank peaked at #9 in 2018, and by 2024 it had eased to #12 with 7,370 births, short of its decade-earlier count by 23% — a milder decline than Alexander's or Michael's, consistent with a name still relatively early in its adoption cycle rather than one fading from a much older peak.

That combination — a very short data history, a single strong namesake, and a comparatively gentle decline — makes Harper's trajectory look less like the long rise-and-fall arcs of Michael or John and more like a recent cultural pick that's still finding its ceiling.

harrison.text: Harrison's best rank came in 1888, at 52. Benjamin Harrison won the presidency that November. Its highest birth count came 128 years later, in 2016, at 3,662 — one of the widest gaps between rank peak and count peak anywhere on this site, and evidence that the name has had two entirely separate lives. The current position is 2,958 births at rank 121, down only 8% over ten years, so the second wave is flattening rather than collapsing. Harrison Ford, born 1942, is the dominant modern association by a distance. Prince Archie, born 2019, appears through his second name, and Edward Norton through his middle. With 96,366 births spread across every decade since 1880, this is a name that has never been rare and never been dominant.

hayden.text:
6,470 births in 2006 was Hayden's count high; the rank followed a year later, #71 in 2007. The pullback since has been comparatively gentle, 19%, though 2,337 births and #154 in 2024 sits well off that mid-2000s peak.

Overall, 144,513 people have been given this name since 1880, a comfortably mid-sized history for this batch.

Star Wars's Hayden Christensen and Heroes's Hayden Panettiere anchor it in mid-2000s screen culture; literary scholar Hayden White and footballer Hayden Foxe give it separate academic and sporting weight.

hayes.text: Hayes has climbed 346% over ten years to reach its 2024 records of 2,249 births and rank 160. Its entire cumulative total is 19,546, one of the smallest here despite the name being on the books since 1880 — a century and a half of near-absence followed by a sudden arrival. One namesake is listed, and it is a middle-name match: Denzel Washington, born 1954, is Denzel Hayes Washington Jr. Rutherford B. Hayes, the more obvious historical hook, does not appear. Surname-names ending in a sibilant have had a strong run lately, with Brooks and Wells moving similarly, and Hayes fits that pattern more convincingly than it fits any presidential association.

hazel.text:
Hazel's raw count actually peaked over a century ago, 7,615 births in 1918, and its rank peaked even earlier still, #18 in 1897 — one of the oldest peak years of any name across all three batches. A 120% gain over the past decade has brought it back to 6,401 births in 2024, still short of that 1918 high but closing the gap fast.

The name has been recorded in every decade since 1880, giving it an unbroken run through more than a century of both rise and decline.

Only one namesake shows up in the enrichment data, tennis and squash player Hazel Hotchkiss Wightman, active in the early 20th century — a name whose modern revival, like Eleanor's and Evelyn's in earlier batches, is bringing back a genuinely old-fashioned choice rather than introducing something new.

henry.text:
Henry's 2024 count of 11,547 is an all-time high for the name, edging past its previous best and landing it at #6 nationally — quietly one of the more durable comebacks in the current top ten, since the name spent much of the mid-20th century well off its 1880s-era standing before climbing back.

It's been recorded in every decade since 1880 and has grown 22% over the past ten years, a steady rather than explosive rise. Unlike Theodore's recent breakout, Henry's climb has been gradual, without a single dramatic jump year.

Its famous bearers lean industrial and intellectual rather than entertainment-driven — Henry Ford, Henry Kissinger, Henry David Thoreau, and, more recently, Bill Gates (born William Henry Gates) — a spread that favors substance over celebrity, which fits a name whose modern revival seems to be about restoring an old-fashioned classic rather than chasing a trend.

hudson.text:
At 7,990 births, Hudson's 2024 count is its best yet, a 52% jump over the past decade that's brought it to #22 nationally — one of the more recent entrants to this range of the chart, with barely two famous bearers on record compared to the five-deep lists most established names carry.

The name technically dates to 1880 in SSA data, but its enrichment data only surfaces two notable namesakes: blues musician Lead Belly, born Huddie Ledbetter — an indirect connection at best — and actor Hudson Williams, born 2001, close in age to the current wave of babies given the name. That thinness in cultural reference points is unusual for a name climbing this fast; most rising names in this range (Asher, Luca, Elias) carry a longer or more varied list of namesakes even while newer to popularity.

Hudson reads more like a place-name-turned-first-name — after the river, most likely — than a name tied to any individual, which may explain why its rise hasn't produced the kind of namesake cluster that names like Ethan or Owen have.

hunter.text:
Nothing in this entire eight-batch dataset has fallen faster than Hunter: down 68% over the past decade, well past the previous record, Jacob's and Mason's tied -62%. The name peaked hard in 2000 — 12,538 births, #35 nationally — before that collapse to 2,831 births and #128 by 2024.

This name's grand total sits at 273,451 births since 1880, a substantial history for a fall this steep.

Hunter S. Thompson and Hunter Biden are real bearers; wrestler Triple H's full ring name, Hunter Hearst Helmsley, used it as a first name too.

ian.text:
Ian's rank actually peaked two years before its raw count: #65 in 2003, versus the count's own high of 6,688 births in 2005 — a short reverse lag, the opposite direction from most names in this dataset, where count typically leads rank.

By 2024 it had eased to 4,547 births, down 17% from a decade prior, at #75.

Ian Fleming, Ian McKellen, and Motörhead's Lemmy (born Ian Fraser Kilmister) span espionage fiction, film, and heavy metal — a namesake list with real range for a name whose data history, starting in 1912, is shorter than most names this established.

iris.text:
3,124 births, #71 nationally — fresh records for Iris on both fronts in 2024, up 135% from a decade before.

This one's been quietly in the data since 1880, showing up in every decade without exception, its total now standing at 98,551 births, right up until its very recent acceleration in popularity.

Novelist Iris Murdoch and designer Iris Apfel anchor the name in 20th-century letters and style, while historian Iris Chang extends its reach into scholarship and human rights writing.

isaac.text:
Isaac's rank peaked at #28 in 2013, four years after its raw-count high of 10,274 births in 2007 — a shorter lag than Elizabeth's century-long gap but the same underlying pattern of rank trailing count.

By 2024 its rank had slipped to #40 with 6,498 births, down 35% from ten years before — steeper than Wyatt's decline but milder than Mason's or Jacob's.

Isaac Newton and Isaac Asimov give the name unusually heavyweight scientific associations, joined by Nobel laureate Isaac Bashevis Singer — three separate fields of intellectual achievement attached to one name, a concentration that few others in this batch, aside perhaps from Thomas, can match.

isabella.text:
Isabella's fall from #1 is the steepest of any former chart-topper in this batch: it held the top national rank as recently as 2009, peaked at 22,935 births in 2010, and now sits at #7 with 10,770 in 2024 — a 37% decline over the past decade, on par with Sophia's drop and part of the same broader retreat of early-2010s chart-topping names.

It's been recorded since 1880 and, like Sophia, carries real historical range: the enrichment data's oldest reference is Sojourner Truth's birth name, Isabella Baumfree, a very different association from the name's more recent pop-culture ties through nickname variants like Bella.

That nickname flexibility — Bella Hadid and Bella Ramsey both appear in its famous-bearer list under the shortened form — may be cushioning the decline somewhat, since Isabella functions as both a formal choice and, via Bella, a softer one, giving it two separate routes back into favor even as the full name's raw numbers fall.

isaiah.text:
2006 was Isaiah's high point on both measures at once: 10,459 births, #39 nationally — the same simultaneous-peak shape as Angel, Cameron, and Mila.

The decline since has been steady: 5,250 births in 2024, 31% below its 2014 level, landing at #56.

Alongside the biblical prophet Isaiah, dated to roughly 765 BC, the enrichment data lists philosopher Isaiah Berlin and NBA guard Isaiah Thomas — a name whose ancient religious root sits next to 20th-century intellectual and athletic namesakes, the same antiquity-to-present spread seen in Caleb's and Ezekiel's entries.

isla.text:
Isla's data history runs surprisingly deep for a name that reads as a recent trend: first recorded in 1886, just six years into the dataset, though it stayed minor for well over a century before climbing sharply in the 2020s.

5,367 births in 2024 is 151% more than the name had a decade earlier. Its best-ever rank, #33, arrived in 2023 — two years after the raw count itself topped out at 5,540 in 2021.

Only one namesake appears in the enrichment data, actor Isla Fisher, active since the mid-2000s — a thin cultural anchor, similar to Aiden's or Cooper's, for a name whose modern popularity outpaces its documented associations.

ivan.text: Ivan is down 24% across the decade, at 2,340 births and rank 153, having reached 3,462 births in 2004 and its best placing of 113 in 2012. Present since 1880 with 148,518 births, spread evenly enough that the name has never belonged to one American generation. The bearers run from Ivan I of Moscow, born 1304, through the tennis player Ivan Lendl, born 1960, to the Croatian footballers Rakitić and Perišić. That range is wider than almost any list in these four batches. Ivan's American usage draws on both Slavic and Spanish-speaking families, two routes that rarely overlap, which may explain why its decline has been gentler than the purely Spanish names of Luis and Juan.

ivy.text:
Ivy's 2024 count, 5,323 births, reached a fresh high the same year its rank did too, #36 — a 132% climb from ten years earlier, one of this batch's bigger percentage gains, though still behind bigger risers like Thiago, Rowan, and Isla.

This name's SSA data goes back to 1880, a footnote presence across most of that span before this recent surge.

Only one bearer shows up in the enrichment data, actor Melissa Rauch, whose middle name is Ivy — an indirect namesake rather than someone using it as a given name, leaving Ivy's rapid modern rise, like Aurora's or Mila's before it, without a clear documented cultural trigger.

jace.text:
6,398 births, #66 nationally — Jace's 2013 peak, set on both measures at once. A 51% decline over the following ten years brought it down to 3,113 births and #114 by 2024.

Jace doesn't turn up until 1936, just past the dataset's halfway point; 89,277 births have carried this name in total since.

Actor Jace Norman is the enrichment data's sole namesake, his career beginning right as the name approached its own peak in the early part of the 2010s.

jack.text:
Jack's current #15 ranking sits well below its actual historical peak: 12,802 births in 1927, nearly a century before this data point. But the recent trend line is nearly flat — 8,434 births in 2024 is only 4% below the count from ten years earlier, a rare case in this batch of a name that has stopped declining rather than one still falling.

It's been recorded since 1880 and its most recent local high point, rank #11, came as recently as 2021, suggesting the long post-1920s decline may have leveled off rather than continuing indefinitely, unlike Ava's still-steep 45% ten-year drop.

The famous-bearer list — Jack London, Jack Kerouac, Jack Lemmon, Jack Kilby — leans toward American writers and inventors across the 20th century, a different profile from a name like Liam or Mateo whose namesakes are almost entirely contemporary athletes and entertainers, fitting a name whose core popularity long predates its current famous bearers.

jackson.text:
Jackson's rank has fallen a long way from where it once stood: #14 at its best, back in 2021, down to #35 by 2024, even though the raw-count peak came earlier still, 12,609 births in 2013. A 44% ten-year decline puts it in the middle of this batch's range of losses.

The name has appeared in SSA data continuously since 1880, a long run before the 2010s surge that produced its recent highs.

Painter Jackson Pollock and musician Jackson Browne anchor the name in mid-20th-century American arts, while historian Frederick Jackson Turner reaches back further still — a namesake spread with real depth, unusual for a name whose own popularity only became substantial in the last fifteen years.

jacob.text:
Jacob shares this batch's steepest decline with Mason, also down 62% over the past decade, but arrived there from a different height: it was the #1 boys' name in 1999, its raw count peaking a year earlier at 36,027 births in 1998. Total births run to 984,245 since 1880.

By 2024 it had fallen to #41 with 6,496 births — one of the sharpest reversals of any former #1 name covered across all three batches so far, alongside Isabella's fall from the top in the earlier batch.

The enrichment data's oldest reference for this name is the biblical patriarch, listed with a birth year of roughly 1790 BC — by far the oldest specific date attached to any name in this batch — alongside contemporary figures like former South African president Jacob Zuma.

jade.text: Jade hit rank 80, its highest placing ever, in 2023, twenty-one years after its highest birth count of 3,630 in 2002. Fewer babies, better placing — the field has spread so far that a name can rank higher on less volume. Currently 2,931 births at rank 84, up 23% across the decade, so the recovery is real rather than an artifact. First recorded in 1944, which makes it a post-war arrival, and the 106,429 all-time total is spread across eight decades of steady low-level use. Amy Winehouse, born 1983, appears through her middle name; Jade Ewen and the footballer Jade North are actual bearers. As a gemstone name it sits in the same family as Ruby and Pearl, but its trajectory looks nothing like theirs.

james.text:
James is the name with by far the longest history in this batch — 5,262,396 total US births since 1880, more than ten times Noah's total. It peaked in 1947 at 94,763 births in a single year, a scale no name reaches today because the pool of names parents choose from is so much wider now.

At 11,793 births in 2024, a comparatively mild 18% below its count a decade earlier, it still holds the #5 national rank — remarkable stability for a name that was already the #1 boys' name in 1940, 84 years earlier.

The famous-bearer list reflects that long history: James Joyce, James Cook, James Madison, James Clerk Maxwell — figures spanning three centuries rather than a recent cultural cluster. Few names carry that kind of multi-generational, multi-field presence while still ranking in the current top five.

jameson.text: Jameson has no famous bearers recorded in the enrichment file whatsoever. Not a thin list — an empty one. For a name given to 3,025 boys in 2024 that absence is worth sitting with, because it means the name is carried entirely by sound and by the surname-as-first-name pattern rather than by anyone in particular. Its history is patchy too: first recorded in 1922, then absent from the 1930s entirely before returning and holding steady. The modern shape is a 2019 high of 4,673 births falling back to current levels, though the ten-year trend is still positive at 16%. Rank sits at 117 against a 2019 best of 77. The whiskey is almost certainly doing more work here than any person, and a cumulative 60,430 births confirm this is a name whose entire life has happened recently.

jason.text: Jason's peak is one of the most extreme on the site: 55,636 births in 1977, and rank 2 in 1974. Nothing else in these four batches comes close to that single-year volume. Today the figure is 2,448 births at rank 148, a 56% fall over the decade — a fall from more than fifty thousand a year to under twenty-five hundred. Cumulative total 1,054,860, second only to Sarah across this whole slice. The bearers are almost uniformly actors born in the sixties and seventies — Jason Bateman, born 1969, Jason Statham, Jason Momoa — which is exactly the cohort the 1977 peak produced. A name this concentrated becomes a birth-decade stamp, and no amount of Greek mythology behind it changes that.

jasper.text: One entry in Jasper's namesake list is a cartoon cat. Tom, of Tom and Jerry, is formally Thomas Jasper Cat, and the enrichment file records him with an occupation of mouser and no birth year — the second fictional character to turn up in these lists, after Spider-Man's J. Jonah Jameson. The real bearers are the painter Jasper Johns, born 1930, and Jasper Tudor, born 1431, uncle to Henry VII. The chart is straightforward: up 57% across the decade, currently 2,750 births at rank 133, marginally off its 2023 peak. Recorded from 1880 but accumulating only 60,802 births in total, Jasper follows the same pattern as Graham and Milo — long presence, negligible volume until the current revival of stone and mineral names.

jaxon.text:
Jaxon and Addison, elsewhere in this batch, are tied for the steepest ten-year decline here: both down 53%. Jaxon's own count peaked in 2016 at 8,142; the rank held on two more years, reaching #39 in 2018, before the slide to 3,618 births and #96 by 2024.

The name's own data history starts in 1972, more recent than most established names.

The enrichment data has no namesake to offer — a name that briefly cracked the top 40 nationally without leaving any documented figure behind it.

jayden.text:
Jayden's fall is the sharpest in this batch: 5,134 births in 2024, 60% short of its count from ten years before, at #59 nationally — a long way down from its 2010 peak, when it briefly held #4.

The name's own history is short by comparison to most in this range, first appearing only in 1977 and gaining almost all of its volume within the following three decades.

No famous bearers appear in the enrichment data at all — a name that reached the near-top of the national chart within living memory, without a single documented namesake anywhere in its rise or fall.

jeremiah.text:
Jeremiah's raw count peaked in 2010 at 7,742; the rank caught up the following year, #49 in 2011. From there it's given back 46% across the following decade, settling at 3,702 births and #93 in 2024, with 222,425 total US births carried by this name since 1880.

The biblical prophet dates to roughly 644 BC — younger than Isaiah's 765 BC from an earlier batch but older than Ezekiel's 620 BC — while 17th-century astronomer Jeremiah Horrocks and national security adviser Jake Sullivan (born Jacob Jeremiah Sullivan) anchor more recent bearers.

jett.text: Jett is up 117% across the decade and set both records in 2024, on 2,222 births alongside rank 161. The record opens in 1892, skips the 1900s entirely, and reaches 24,923 births. No namesakes are listed. The name reads as a modern coinage but is not quite one — it exists as a surname, and Joan Jett has carried it publicly since the late 1970s without appearing in this file. What separates Jett from Legend and Stetson, its neighbours in the invented-Americana category, is that it also functions as a plausible short form, which gives it a flexibility the others lack. Single-syllable boys' names ending in a hard consonant have been among the most reliable performers of the past fifteen years.

john.text:
John's total of 5,196,210 births since 1880 edges out Michael's and even James's from the top-25 batch, and like Samuel and William before it, its best-ever rank — #1 — was already locked in by 1880, the first year this dataset covers. Its single biggest year came later, 1947, with 88,321 births.

Today it sits at #21 with 8,047 births in 2024, down 25% over the decade — the same percentage decline as Samuel, though John's much larger historical base means the absolute drop represents a bigger swing in real terms.

The famous-bearer list spans philosophy (John Locke), literature (J. R. R. Tolkien, born John Ronald Reuel Tolkien), and politics (John F. Kennedy, John Adams) across four centuries — a name whose cultural weight was already fully established well before the 20th-century birth boom that produced its highest single-year count.

jonah.text: Jonah is the flattest name in this batch: down 1% over ten years, which within measurement noise is no movement at all. Its birth count high of 2,981 came in 2008 and its rank high of 124 in 2023, and today's 2,879 births at rank 126 sit within touching distance of both. Almost nothing has happened here in twenty years. One entry in the bearer list deserves a flag: J. Jonah Jameson is a fictional newspaper publisher from Spider-Man, recorded with no birth year and an occupation of philanthropist, which is doubly wrong. Jonah Hill, born 1983, and the rugby player Jonah Lomu are real. On the books since 1880 and 83,176 births deep, this is a biblical name that has found a level and stayed there.

jonathan.text:
24,348 births and #15 — Jonathan's count and rank hit their marks in the exact same year, 1988. Since then 51% has come off the count, leaving 4,018 births and #83 nationally by 2024.

870,561 US babies have carried this name since 1880, a serious historical footprint for a name that's now well off its late-1980s standing.

Jonathan Swift roots it in 18th-century satire; Jon Voight and Orlando Bloom, a generation apart, keep it current on screen; and physicist David Gross carries the full given name into contemporary science.

jordan.text:
16,137 births in 1990 was Jordan's count peak; #26, its best rank, took another seven years to show up, in 1997. Since then it's given back 52% across the following decade, landing at 3,326 births and #104 nationally in 2024, one of the steeper declines in this batch.

Over half a million US births trace to this name since 1880, real historical weight for something now sitting well outside the top 50.

Cultural critic Jordan Peterson and footballer Jordan Henderson dominate the namesake list — entirely 21st-century figures despite the name's much older data history.

jose.text:
592,999 US births have carried this name since the dataset's 1880 start, a substantial historical footprint. The count topped out at 12,868 in 2002; the rank needed two more years to catch up, hitting #28 in 2004.

Thirty-one percent lower than a decade ago — that's where 2024 lands, 3,768 births and #91 nationally.

Nobel laureate José Saramago, Uruguay's former president José Mujica, and Cuban independence figure José Martí give the name deep literary and political weight across Spanish-speaking countries and three separate centuries.

joseph.text:
Joseph shows the widest gap in this batch between when its rank peaked and when its raw count peaked: rank hit #5 all the way back in 1912, but the actual count didn't reach its high of 32,748 until 1956 — a 44-year lag, far longer than the four-or-five-year gaps seen in Ethan or David, meaning Joseph was proportionally more dominant among a much smaller pool of names in 1912 than it ever was at its later numerical peak.

Total births since 1880 run to 2,672,746. In 2024 it counted 7,223 births, 41% fewer than a decade earlier, landing it at #32 nationally.

The famous-bearer list bridges entertainment and politics unusually directly — Michael Jackson (born Michael Joseph Jackson), Joe Biden (born Joseph Robinette Biden), Pope Benedict XVI (born Joseph Ratzinger) — three very different kinds of public figures who all carry Joseph as a given rather than middle name.

josephine.text:
Josephine's rank actually peaked before its count did — #21 in 1916, two years ahead of the raw-count record, 8,682 births in 1918. More than a century later, the name is climbing again: 64% growth over the last decade, reaching 3,746 births in 2024.

This name's own total, 328,296 births, has accumulated since the dataset's 1880 start.

Josephine Baker's jazz-age fame anchors it in the 1920s, while Belgian singer Angèle, born Angèle Van Laeken, has it tucked into her own birth name as well, in contemporary pop music.

joshua.text:
Joshua carries one of the longest lags in this entire batch between its count peak and its rank peak: the raw count hit its high, 44,099 births, in 1989, but the rank didn't reach its own best, #3, until 2002 — thirteen years later, just ahead of Zoe's twelve-year gap.

1,249,012 total births since 1880 makes Joshua roughly as historically large as Charles, though its recent trajectory looks nothing alike: 5,244 births in 2024 is 52% below its count ten years earlier, closer to Emily's steep pace than to Charles's milder retreat.

Joshua Reynolds anchors the name in 18th-century British portraiture, while Josh Hutcherson and Josh Hartnett keep a shortened form current in contemporary film — two very different eras represented under variations of the same name.

josiah.text:
Josiah's rank peaked at #45 in 2019, two years after its raw-count high of 7,073 births in 2017 — a short lag similar to Isla's pattern later in this same batch.

The decline since has been moderate: 5,457 births in 2024, only 16% under its count ten years prior — one of the milder ten-year drops in this batch, alongside Charles's 24%.

Its famous-bearer list runs entirely through 18th- and 19th-century intellectual figures — physicist Josiah Willard Gibbs, ceramicist Josiah Wedgwood, philosopher Josiah Royce — with no contemporary entry at all, an old-fashioned namesake profile that matches the name's steady, unspectacular modern trajectory.

josie.text: Josie has grown 125% in ten years and is at its all-time high of 2,893 births, rank 88. Like Millie, it is a diminutive that stopped being short for anything — Josephine's formal register is not required for Josie to work now. On the books since 1880, with 72,858 births accumulated, most of it recent. The enrichment file lists exactly one bearer, the model Josie Maran, born 1978, who has no plausible connection to the current rise. That thin association is the point: names in this cohort are moving on sound and shape rather than on anyone famous. Compare Millie, where a single actor explains most of the curve. Josie has climbed nearly as hard with nobody attached, which suggests the underlying pattern is doing the work.

juan.text: Juan has the largest cumulative total of the three Spanish names here, at 366,010 births since 1880, and the steepest decline: down 33% over ten years, from 8,230 births in 2005 to 2,601 today, with its best rank of 46 set in 1999. Every one of these names peaked between 1999 and 2007 and has fallen together since. The bearers reach back furthest of any list in this batch — John of the Cross, born 1542 — and forward to Juan Guaidó, born 1983, with Juan Perón, born 1895, in between. Jean Reno, born 1948, is filed here under his birth name Juan Moreno. As with Carlos, the entries are real but the forms vary by language, so the list reads as looser than it is.

jude.text: Jude is one of the quieter names in this slice: down 12% over ten years, sitting at 2,284 births and rank 156, having topped out at 2,668 births in 2015 and rank 151 in 2021. Nothing dramatic in either direction. The bearer file reaches further back than most, to Jude the Apostle, listed with a birth year of 10, which is about as early as this dataset goes. Jude Law, born 1972, and the footballer Jude Bellingham, born 2003, carry the modern association. Patsy Kensit appears on a middle-name match. Recorded from 1912 with 54,503 births banked, Jude has the Beatles song working in its favour and a short, closed sound that has aged better than most of its 1960s contemporaries.

julia.text: Julia held rank 26 in 1880, then recorded its busiest year over a century later, 8,838 births in 2001 — one of very few names that were both genuinely Victorian and genuinely popular a century later. That double life is reflected in 475,798 births accumulated since records began. The current position is 2,359 births at rank 116, a 35% ten-year decline. Its bearers are unusually distinguished and unusually varied: Julia Child, born 1912, filed here with an occupation of typist, which undersells her considerably; Julia Kristeva, Julia Gillard, Julia Roberts. Julie Andrews, born 1935, appears under a different form. Latin in origin and stable in spelling, Julia has avoided the fragmentation that splits Allison and Hailey across four variants each.

julian.text:
Julian is at its best-ever rank right now: #30 in 2024, exactly matching its peak, with a birth count that's held nearly flat over the past decade — down just 4% — one of the smallest ten-year swings covered in this batch.

This name appears in every US decade of data from 1880 onward, and its raw-count peak came in 2017 at 8,451 births — a gentle decline since, to 7,368 in 2024, rather than any sharp drop.

The famous-bearer list runs from 19th-century polish nobility-adjacent naming through to WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange and Nobel physicist Julian Schwinger — a spread across politics, science, and literature (Julian Barnes) that doesn't lean toward any single decade the way Camila's or Dylan's lists do.

juniper.text: Juniper has the smallest cumulative total of any name across these four batches: 19,452 births in its entire recorded history, which begins in 1969. It has grown 279% over the decade and set its best rank of 111 in 2024, on 2,441 births. No namesakes are recorded at all. That combination — high current volume, negligible history, nobody attached — puts it in the same category as Everly and Juniper's fellow botanicals, where the name is chosen purely for sound and connotation. Plant names have moved as a block alongside Sage, Willow and Ivy. The specific risk is that blocks like this tend to date together, so a Juniper born now will read as precisely 2020s in the way an Autumn reads as 1990s.

kai.text:
Kai's count and rank peaked together in 2022 — 5,366 births and #59 nationally — before easing to 4,276 and #76 by 2024, a 77% rise over the full decade despite that recent pullback.

The enrichment data attributes a German origin to the name, a less obvious root than the Hawaiian or East Asian associations it's often assumed to carry, and its data history starts in 1926, later than most established names but well before its recent popularity.

Physicist Kai Siegbahn and footballer Kai Havertz anchor the name in science and sport respectively, two fields with little else in common beyond sharing this one short name.

kayden.text: Kayden has no recorded namesakes and no listed origin, and the name surfaces in SSA records only in 1989. Among names given to nearly three thousand American boys a year, that combination is close to unique — this is a constructed name, assembled from the sounds of Aiden and Hayden rather than inherited from anywhere. The arc is now clearly downward: a 2014 high of 4,741 births at rank 90, falling to 2,882 at rank 125, a 39% decline over ten years. The entire all-time total of 78,924 has accumulated in about thirty-five years. Names built primarily from a popular rhyme tend to fall as fast as they rose, because what carried them up was a sound pattern rather than any particular meaning, and sound patterns date quickly.

kennedy.text: Kennedy enters SSA data in 1957, four years before the inauguration that made the surname a household word, and the timing is hard to read as coincidence. What is more surprising is where it landed: the name is now predominantly given to girls, an unusual destination for a political surname. Its high was 4,522 births in 2015 with a best rank of 54 the year before; it now records 2,881 at rank 89, down 36% across the decade. The all-time total of 98,080 has accumulated almost entirely since the 1990s. The bearer list is a mix of middle-name matches and family connections — Vince McMahon, born 1945, the journalist Tatiana Schlossberg — rather than people known primarily by the name. Surname-names tend to fade with the memory that produced them.

kinsley.text: Kinsley's rank high of 57 came in 2021, four years after its birth-count high of 4,051 in 2017 — the field thinning underneath it rather than the name growing. Today it sits at 2,929 births and rank 85, still up 20% across the decade despite being well off both peaks. First recorded in 1978, with 47,526 births banked and no namesakes listed at all. Structurally it belongs with Kennedy and Everly: a surname shape, a -ley ending, no particular person attached. What separates it from Kayden, which is falling hard, is that the -ley pattern has aged better than the -aden one so far. Whether that holds is genuinely open, since neither pattern has anything anchoring it beyond current taste.

lainey.text:
No name across all five batches so far has grown faster than Lainey: 901% over the past decade, taking it to 5,147 births in 2024, a fresh high on both count and rank at #38.

That figure is almost entirely a small-base effect. Total US births under this name run to just 22,674 since it first appeared in 1968 — smaller than Thiago's total from the fourth batch — and its rank only cracked the top 50 this year for the first time.

The enrichment data lists no origin and no famous bearers, leaving one of this dataset's steepest-ever growth curves without a single traceable explanation.

landon.text:
Near-top-tier once: 10,483 births and #33 nationally, both in 2010. Since then it's shed 60% across the following ten years, one of the steepest ten-year falls in this whole dataset, landing at 3,316 births and #106 by 2024.

184,879 babies have carried this name in total, dating to 1882 — a substantial history for one that's now fallen this hard.

Soccer star Landon Donovan and Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker, whose middle name is Landon, round out a short namesake list for a name now well past its 2010 heyday.

layla.text:
Layla's data history starts later than most in this batch, in 1950 — two decades before Eric Clapton's 1970 song of the same name, meaning the name was already in quiet US use well before that cultural moment, contrary to what its popularity might suggest.

2019 marked its high point on both fronts together: 6,518 births, #23 nationally. It's eased since to 5,305 births and #37 by 2024, an 18% pullback from a decade prior.

The enrichment data's only listed bearer is professional wrestler Layla El, active since the mid-2000s, decades after the name's actual first appearance in the birth data.

leah.text:
6,790 births in 2009 was Leah's count peak; #24, the rank's own best, followed a year later. It's fallen 29% over the past decade since, to 3,969 births and #53 in 2024.

1730 BC is the oldest date in Leah's enrichment data, the biblical Leah — older than Hannah's and Delilah's references elsewhere in this batch, and behind only Jacob's 1790 BC from the third batch as the most ancient figure attached to any name across every batch so far.

Rashida Jones and Leah Remini keep the name current in film and TV; footballer Leah Williamson extends it into sport.

legend.text: Legend is a word before it is a name, and the data reflects how recently it became the latter: first recorded in 1993, 24,856 births altogether, neither origin nor namesakes on file. It has grown 336% across the decade, topping out during 2021 on 3,182 births alongside rank 118. Today: 2,275 and rank 157, already off that high. The obvious association, the musician John Legend, is itself a stage name, so even the likely source is not a bearer in any real sense. Aspirational word-names such as this and Serenity share a structural weakness: they promise something specific, and taste in what parents want to promise turns over faster than taste in sounds does.

leilani.text:
3,354 births in 2024, up 118% from ten years earlier — though the name's actual best year, 3,866 births, was two years prior, in 2022, alongside its best-ever rank, #59.

Nothing shows up before 1917 in this name's records, well over three decades after the dataset begins.

No famous bearers turn up anywhere in the enrichment data for Leilani, and its enrichment origin field is blank too — a name with almost no documented cultural trail despite its steady climb.

leo.text:
Leo has already cooled from a very recent high: its rank peaked at #18 in 2023, just one year before this data ends, and by 2024 it had slipped to #24 even though the raw count, 7,793, is still close to its 2022 peak of 8,290. A 96% rise over the decade is one of the larger gains in this batch, but the rank slippage suggests the climb may already be leveling off.

The name has been recorded since 1880, giving it a longer paper trail than its recent surge might suggest, similar in shape to Asher's pattern of old roots and a recent breakout.

Its famous-bearer list is dominated by French cultural figures under the accented spelling Léo — composer Léo Delibes, singer Johnny Hallyday (born Jean-Philippe Léo Smet) — pointing to a European namesake pool quite different from the largely American or British lists attached to names like Hudson or Owen.

leon.text: Leon has nearly returned to a peak it set a hundred years ago. Its highest birth count, 2,677, dates to 1924; it currently records 2,547, up 136% across the decade. Very few names manage that kind of round trip — most Victorian and interwar names either stay buried or come back at a fraction of their old volume. Rank tells a different story, 73 back in 1926 against 141 now, because the field is so much wider today. Present since 1880 with 181,458 births. The namesakes are almost entirely French and nineteenth-century: the physicist Léon Foucault, born 1819, the prime ministers Léon Blum and Léon Bourgeois, and Léon Gambetta — all spelled with an accent that American records drop.

leonardo.text:
4,425 births in 2019 was Leonardo's high point by count; the rank followed three years later, reaching #75 in 2022. Growth over the decade has been modest, 15%, landing at 3,951 births in 2024.

The record here has a genuine gap — first appearing in 1885, then nothing at all through the 1890s, before resuming in the 1900s and continuing steadily since.

Leonardo da Vinci and mathematician Fibonacci, born Leonardo Bonacci, give this name roots stretching back nearly 900 years; Leonardo DiCaprio carries it into contemporary Hollywood.

levi.text:
Levi is a smaller-scale name than most in this batch but a stable one: it peaked in 2022 at 9,861 births and sits at 9,513 in 2024, essentially flat over the past year and up 18% over the full decade — growth without the sharp swings seen in Theodore or Mateo.

The name has been recorded since 1880 and has held a fairly consistent, modest presence through most of that history, only recently climbing into the current top 12 rather than arriving as a sudden new entrant.

Its most commercially famous bearer, Levi Strauss, ties the name to 19th-century American manufacturing rather than entertainment or sport, an unusual anchor point among current top-15 names' famous-bearer lists, most of which lean toward recent actors or athletes like Zachary Levi, who also appears here as a more contemporary reference.

liam.text:
Liam is currently in the unusual position of being both the most popular boy's name in America and still growing — 22,164 births in 2024, its highest count ever, up 20% over the past decade. That's a different shape than most names at the top of the chart, which tend to be sliding down from an earlier peak even while holding rank.

The name barely existed as a US birth record before the late 1940s and didn't take off until decades later, originally as the Irish short form of William before becoming a name in its own right. It's held the #1 spot continuously since 2017, which is a long run by modern standards, when turnover at the top used to happen every few years.

Its famous bearers skew recent and specific — Liam Payne, Liam Hemsworth, Formula One's Liam Lawson — which suggests the name's rise tracks a generation of parents naming after people roughly their own age rather than historical figures, a pattern that's less common among older top-ranked names like James or William.

liliana.text: Liliana set its record in 2024, with 3,009 births and rank 80 both marking all-time bests. Its history is short by the standards of this batch — nothing before 1950, which puts it among the newer arrivals here alongside Kayden and Kinsley, though it has climbed far more steadily than either. Ten-year growth of 14% is unspectacular but consistent, and 71,993 births in aggregate reflect a name that has accumulated gradually rather than spiking. The namesakes are Italian and serious: the director Liliana Cavani, born 1933, and Liliana Segre, born 1930, a Holocaust survivor and Italian senator. The enrichment file also lists Lilian Harvey, born 1906, under a different spelling entirely, which is a reminder that these lists match loosely and shouldn't be read as a roll of exact bearers.

lillian.text:
10,049 births in 1920 marked Lillian's high point by count — but the rank had already hit its own best, #10, twenty-two years earlier in 1898, a reverse gap similar in direction to Charlie's, if smaller. The fall since has been steep: 44% lower across the following decade, settling at 3,882 births and #54 in 2024.

Close to half a million US births carry this name since 1880, placing it among this batch's larger names by history.

Lillian Gish and Lillian Hellman anchor it in early-to-mid-20th-century film and literature; industrial engineer Lillian Moller Gilbreth adds a scientific namesake from roughly the same era.

lily.text:
Lily's rank and count peaked together in 2011 — #15 nationally and 8,192 births — one of this batch's cleaner simultaneous peaks alongside Carter's and Chloe's.

Since then it's eased to #24 with 6,093 births in 2024, down just 10% over the past decade — a notably mild decline for a name that peaked well over a decade ago, milder than Chloe's 25% drop from a similarly-timed high.

The famous-bearer list mixes music (Lily Allen), film (Lily Collins, Lily James), comedy (Lily Tomlin), and fiction (Harry Potter's Lily Potter) — a broad spread across entertainment that gives the name wide contemporary visibility even as its raw numbers have settled into a slow, gradual decline.

lincoln.text:
Lincoln's rank and count moved apart by three years: 8,201 births in 2017 was the raw-count high, while #40, the best rank, took until 2020 to show up.

The past decade has been nearly flat since — down just 5% to 4,567 births in 2024, one of the mildest ten-year moves in this batch alongside Nolan's 6% dip.

Polar explorer Lincoln Ellsworth and Rhode Island politician Lincoln Chafee carry the name as a given name, while the enrichment data's inclusion of Lincoln Ellsworth's exact birth year, 1880, ties one namesake directly to the very first year this dataset covers.

logan.text:
Logan has the steepest ten-year decline in this entire batch: down 54% since a decade ago, to 6,267 births in 2024, dropping it to #46 — well below most other names covered here. Its raw count peaked earlier, in 2007 at 15,330, and its best-ever rank, #5, came a full decade later in 2017, the same delayed-rank pattern seen in Ethan and David, before the recent sharp fall.

This name has appeared in every decade of US data since 1880, a long history before its 21st-century surge and subsequent retreat.

The famous-bearer list mixes fiction and reality in an unusual way: the Marvel character Wolverine (real name Logan, per the enrichment data's "born" field of 1832) sits alongside YouTuber Logan Paul and Formula One's Logan Sargeant — a spread from 19th-century comic-book backstory to 21st-century internet fame that no other name in this batch quite matches.

lorenzo.text: Lorenzo is at its all-time high right now. The 3,044 births recorded in 2024 are the most in any year since counting began in 1880, and rank 116 is likewise its best showing. That is rare in this batch — most names here peaked years ago and are managing decline. Growth of 85% over the decade puts it among the strongest risers. The namesake list is almost comically Renaissance: Lorenzo de' Medici, born 1449, the philologist Lorenzo Valla, born 1407, and Gian Lorenzo Bernini. Clement XII, born 1652, was christened Lorenzo Corsini before taking a papal name. That weight of association gives the name something Jameson and Kayden lack entirely — a genuine pre-modern history — while the 82,979 all-time total shows American usage stayed thin for most of that span.

luca.text:
Luca is the fastest-growing name in this batch by a wide margin: 245% higher than a decade earlier, with both its raw count and its rank hitting new highs in the same year, 2024 — 7,959 births, its best ever, at #23 nationally, with no sign yet of a peak behind it.

Its history is unusually broken up: first recorded in 1915, with activity that then skips the 1930s and 1950s entirely — two full decades with fewer than five US births — before resuming and eventually taking off in the 2010s and 2020s. Few names in this range show that kind of on-again, off-again presence across a century of data.

Its famous bearers lean heavily Italian and historical — Renaissance mathematician Luca Pacioli, painter Luca Signorelli — alongside recent figures like director Luca Guadagnino and footballer Luca Toni, a spread that tracks the name's Italian origin more closely than most of its English-origin neighbors in this batch.

lucas.text:
Lucas has had one of the more gradual, low-volatility trajectories in this batch: it peaked in 2017 at 13,029 births. Ten years on, 10,703 births in 2024 puts it just 12% below that mark — a smaller pullback than most of its early-2010s-peaking peers like Isabella or Sophia, holding at #9 nationally.

The name dates back to 1881 in SSA records and has been present in every decade since, longer continuous use than several other names currently ranked above it, like Theodore or Mateo, even though it now sits slightly lower on the chart.

Its famous-bearer list includes figures across thirteen centuries of use — Luke the Evangelist's association at one end, contemporary footballers Lucas Vázquez and Lucas Hernández at the other — with Lucas Cranach the Elder's Renaissance-era art in between, a name that has apparently never gone fully out of circulation long enough to become strongly associated with any single era.

lucia.text: Lucia set both its records in 2024 — 2,658 births, rank 98 — after growing 85% across the decade. Saint Lucy, born 283, appears in the file with her occupation left blank, the entry stripped down to a name and a date, which is what happens when a bearer predates most of the categories the data was built for. The other listed names are a loose international scatter: the actor Lucia Bosè, born 1931, the badminton player Susi Susanti, the Body Shop founder Anita Roddick. Recorded from 1880 with 56,400 births in total, Lucia has spent most of its American life as an Italian and Spanish family name rather than a mainstream choice, and its current rise reflects the same broadening that has lifted Lorenzo and Matteo.

lucy.text:
Lucy's 2024 count, 5,396 births, is its highest ever, matched by a fresh best-ever rank, #34 — a 26% climb over the past decade, a steadier pace than the triple-digit gains posted by names like Ivy or Ezekiel in this same batch.

This name's SSA data reaches back to 1880, though its enrichment data goes back further still: Saint Lucy, dated to roughly the year 283, is one of the oldest specific figures attached to any name covered across all four batches.

Lucy Liu and Lucy Lawless keep the name visible in contemporary film and television, while Lucy Maud Montgomery's authorship of Anne of Green Gables adds a literary anchor from over a century ago.

luis.text: Luis has fallen 29% over the past decade, sliding from 8,054 births in 2007 to 2,778, its best rank of 49 having been reached back in 2000. That is a substantial retreat for a name with 291,974 births behind it. The pattern matches Carlos and Juan almost exactly — all three Spanish staples peaked around the turn of the century and have declined together since, which points to a shift in naming among Hispanic American families rather than anything specific to any one name. The bearers are genuinely international: Jorge Luis Borges, born 1899, the physicist Luis Walter Alvarez, born 1911, and the footballer Luis Suárez. Ronaldo appears because Luís is among his given names, which is a stretch even by the loose standards of these lists.

luka.text:
A 648% surge over the past decade — driven almost entirely by a tiny starting base — brought Luka to fresh highs on both measures in 2024: 3,697 births, #94 nationally. Total US births under this name run to just 25,604 since 1975, when it first entered the data.

That combination of a recent start and outsized percentage growth matches the shape seen in Thiago and Theo from earlier batches.

Basketball star Luka Dončić and football captain Luka Modrić dominate the namesake list — both born within roughly fifteen years of each other, both at the top of their respective sports.

luke.text:
Luke is one of the few names in this batch where the raw-count peak and the rank peak landed in exactly the same year: 2014, both times — a cleaner, simultaneous high point than the multi-year lags seen in Ethan, David, or Matthew.

Since then it's fallen to #34 with 7,039 births in 2024, down 33% over the decade, a decline in the middle of this batch's range — steeper than Julian's near-flat trend but milder than Logan's steep drop.

Its most culturally prominent association carries no real birth year at all: Luke Skywalker's enrichment entry lists "born: null," a fictional character whose influence on the name's popularity can't be measured the same way as a real namesake. The name's other bearers — footballer Luke Shaw, actors Luke Perry and Luke Evans — are all real, contemporary figures rather than the older names one might expect for something this established.

luna.text:
Luna's rise is one of the sharpest in this batch: a 205% increase over the past decade, though its best-ever rank, #10, was reached in 2022 and has already eased to #13 by 2024 — a recent pullback similar to Leo's and Owen's, following a period of very fast growth.

Unusually for a name of Latin origin with data going back to 1880, its only listed famous bearer is fictional: Luna Lovegood, from the Harry Potter series, whose Wikidata "born" year of 1981 refers to the character's story timeline rather than a real person. That's a different kind of namesake than any other entry in this batch carries.

Whether that fictional association is driving the name's recent surge isn't something the birth data alone can confirm, but Luna's growth curve — old roots, a long quiet period, then a sudden climb — matches the shape of several other recently-popular names here, like Asher and Santiago.

lydia.text: Lydia's best rank of 75 dates to 1883, while its highest birth count came in 2014 — a gap of 131 years, the widest in this batch and among the widest anywhere on the site. It has fallen 27% since that recent peak, to 2,663 births at rank 97, with 184,572 births accumulated since 1880. The bearer list is unusually literary and unusually international: Lydia Maria Child, born 1802, an abolitionist writer; the Estonian poet Lydia Koidula, born 1843; the novelist Lydia Davis. Liliʻuokalani, born 1838, the last monarch of Hawaii, appears under her baptismal name Lydia. Of Greek origin and biblical in use, Lydia has never been fashionable enough to become dated, which is a durable position to hold.

lyla.text: Lyla is at its peak right now — 2,944 births in 2024, rank 83, both records. The odd detail is how long it took. The name surfaces in 1884 and has technically shown up in every decade from then on, but the all-time total is only 46,190, which means well over a century of near-invisibility followed by a recent climb of 24% in ten years. No namesakes are recorded and no origin is listed. Functionally it operates as a respelling of Lila or a shortening of Delilah, and its rise tracks the broader preference for short vowel-heavy girls' names that also lifted Mila and Ayla. Names that peak on their most recent data point are the hardest to forecast, because nothing in the chart yet shows what the ceiling looks like.

madeline.text: Madeline peaked in 1998 at 5,869 births and rank 50, and has been drifting down ever since without ever falling sharply. It records 2,907 births at rank 87 today, off 16% across ten years — a gentle slope compared with Nicholas or Audrey. The all-time total of 204,520 makes it the third-largest here, built steadily across every decade since 1880. Its bearers are almost entirely performers and writers: Madeline Kahn, born 1942, the novelist Madeline Miller, born 1978, and several actors. Competition from Madelyn, Madeleine and Madilyn splits the sound across spellings, so the true frequency of the name as heard is higher than any single line on this chart shows — a problem that affects every name with a contested spelling.

madelyn.text:
Madelyn's rank peaked well after its count: 4,566 births in 2008, then #58 fifteen years later in 2023 — one of the longer count-to-rank gaps in this batch. The ten-year trend is a mild 22% decline, to 3,364 births in 2024.

This name's history starts in 1890, a decade later than the dataset's opening, and its total US births now reach 112,677 over that span.

Actor Madelyn Cline, whose career began well after the name's own 2008 peak, is the only namesake the enrichment data offers.

madison.text:
Madison's 56% decline over the past decade ranks third-steepest in this batch, behind Jayden and Andrew. 2001 was its high point on both fronts: 22,166 births, #2 nationally — a genuine near-chart-topping run that's since fallen to 4,563 births and #46 in 2024.

Unusually for a name this large, its data history doesn't reach back to 1880 at all — the first recorded year is 1970, a full 90 years into the dataset, among the shortest histories of any major name covered so far.

Its famous-bearer list is almost entirely young performers born in the late 1990s — Madison Beer, Madison Iseman, Madison Pettis — a generational cluster with no older reference point at all.

maeve.text:
378% — no name in this batch climbed faster than Maeve over the past decade, hitting 3,098 births in 2024, though its best-ever rank, #73, actually arrived a year earlier, in 2023.

Just 26,442 people have carried this name in the US total, dating only to 1940, a small base that helps explain such an outsized percentage swing.

Novelist Maeve Binchy, active from the 1980s on, is the enrichment data's only namesake — a single Irish literary figure behind a name whose American popularity is entirely recent.

malachi.text: Malachi has not moved at all: 0% change over ten years, the flattest reading in these four batches, ahead even of Jonah's marginal decline. It records 2,404 births at rank 149, against 2,776 births at its 2006 high, with its strongest placing of 146 coming as recently as 2023. Present since 1880, 63,291 births accumulated, and no namesakes listed whatsoever. For a minor prophet with a book of the Bible to his name, that absence is odd, and it reflects a general gap in the enrichment data around biblical figures who are not also historical celebrities. Total stability across a decade is genuinely rare in this dataset; most names are visibly rising or falling, and Malachi is doing neither.

margaret.text: At 1,266,052 births, Margaret is the largest name across all four of these batches — more than a quarter of a million ahead of Sarah. Rank 3 came in 1891; the busiest single year was 1921, at 28,468 births. What makes it remarkable is the present tense: up 18% across ten years, reaching 2,303 births and rank 119. Almost nothing else with this much historical weight is currently growing. The bearers are formidable — Margaret Thatcher, born 1925, Margaret Atwood, Margaret Mead, Margaret Mitchell — and Sally Field, born 1946, appears through her middle name. Margaret's advantage is its supply of usable short forms; Maggie, Peggy, Meg and Greta let one formal name serve several quite different registers.

maria.text:
An 11-year gap separates Maria's two peaks: 10,147 births in 1964 by raw count, #30 by rank in 1975. The recent trend is a modest 12% gain across the last ten years, to 3,105 births in 2024.

The grand total, 567,411 births since 1880, ranks among the larger figures in this batch.

Marie Curie and Corazon Aquino, the Philippines' first female president, give the name real scientific and political weight across the 20th century, alongside Polish Nobel poet Wisława Szymborska.

mason.text:
Mason's decline is tied for the steepest in this batch: down 62% over the past decade, matching Jacob's drop exactly. Its rank and count peaked together in 2011 — #2 nationally and 19,528 births — meaning the fall from a near-chart-topping position has been unusually fast, from #2 to #42 in roughly a decade.

This name's SSA data runs back to 1880, a long history before its 2010s spike and subsequent retreat.

Its famous-bearer list is almost entirely contemporary football — Mason Mount, Mason Greenwood, Mason Holgate — young English players rather than any older reference, a name whose recent popularity clearly outpaced any prior cultural association it might have carried.

mateo.text:
Mateo is the fastest-moving name in this batch relative to its size: a 202% rise over the past decade, second only to Theodore's growth rate, taking it from a niche choice to #7 nationally with 11,302 births in 2024, its highest count on record.

It first appears in SSA data in 1904 but stayed a minor presence for most of the following century, meaning almost all of its current volume has arrived in the last twenty years. That makes Mateo one of the more recent additions to the top ten by total-history standards, alongside Ezra.

Its famous bearers are almost entirely contemporary and international — footballers Mateo Kovačić and Mateo Retegui, both active professionals rather than historical figures — a contrast with names like James or William whose namesake lists stretch back centuries. That skew toward recent, globally visible figures fits a name whose US popularity is itself a recent development tied to broader interest in Spanish-language names.

matias.text: Matias grew 305% across the decade and reached its best figures in 2024, at 2,263 births and rank 158. Listed as Finnish in origin, which is accurate but incomplete — the name is at least as common in Spanish-speaking countries, usually written Matías with an accent the American data drops. Recorded from 1904, 23,249 births total. Every listed bearer holds it as a middle name: Kimi Räikkönen, born 1979, is Kimi-Matias; the footballers Gonçalo Ramos and Ezequiel Schelotto likewise. Matias is rising alongside Mateo and Matteo, three forms of the same underlying name occupying three separate lines in this dataset, which is the clearest possible demonstration of how spelling fragments the record.

matteo.text: Matteo reached its best-ever figures in 2024: 2,582 births, rank 138. Growth of 209% across the decade makes it one of the fastest risers here, and its cumulative 31,026 births are among the slimmest in this slice, so nearly everyone who has ever carried the name in America is currently young. Recorded from 1911 with no listed origin, though the Italian derivation is obvious. Exactly one namesake appears, the footballer Mattéo Guendouzi, born 1999, spelled with an accent the American data does not use. Matteo belongs with Lorenzo and Lucia in the group of Italian names moving up together — a broadening of taste rather than any individual's influence, since none of the three has a bearer prominent enough to drive it.

matthew.text:
Matthew shows this batch's longest lag between a raw-count peak and a rank peak: it peaked at 50,208 births in 1983 but didn't reach its best-ever rank, #2, until 1995 — twelve years later, even longer than Joseph's 44-year gap in absolute terms is proportionally shorter given Matthew's peak came in living memory rather than a century ago.

By 2024 it had fallen to 7,078 births, 45% below its count a decade prior, landing it at #33 nationally — a steeper decline than John's or Samuel's, closer to Michael's or Ethan's pace.

Its famous-bearer list leans heavily toward film and music from the past several decades — Matt Damon, Matthew McConaughey, Matthew Perry, plus Sting (born Gordon Matthew Thomas Sumner) — a modern, entertainment-heavy cluster that contrasts with the centuries-spanning lists attached to older names like David or John.

maverick.text:
No name in this batch grew faster than Maverick: 252% over the past decade, this name only entering SSA records at all in 1957 and staying a minor presence for decades before its recent surge to 6,615 births and #36 nationally in 2024, a new high just two years after its actual peak count of 7,047 in 2022.

Its enrichment data lists exactly one namesake, motorcycle racer Maverick Viñales — no deep historical anchor the way Wyatt has in Wyatt Earp.

Between the recent data start, the single contemporary namesake, and the sheer growth rate, Maverick reads as the newest and least historically rooted name in this entire batch — a modern coinage rather than a name with any pre-20th-century use to speak of.

maya.text:
Maya's 7% ten-year gain lands almost exactly where Micah's does, though the paths differ: Maya's count peaked back in 2006 at 5,047, while the rank kept improving until 2023, reaching #50 — seventeen years after the count's own high point.

Records for this name begin in 1940, sixty years into the dataset — later than the oldest established names, earlier than several fresh arrivals in this same batch.

Maya Angelou gives it 20th-century literary weight; Maya Rudolph and Maya Hawke keep it current in comedy and film.

melanie.text: Melanie peaked on count and rank simultaneously in 1972, hitting 6,295 births and rank 42 together, then losing 39% across the past ten years to land on 2,244 births and rank 122. The record opens in 1886 and totals 261,158 births. Every listed bearer is French, each written with an accent that American records drop: Mélanie Laurent, born 1983, Mélanie Thierry, the composer Mélanie Bonis, born 1858. That the file contains no Anglophone Melanie at all is striking for a name this common in the United States, and it reflects a broader bias in the enrichment source toward European figures. The 1972 peak sits within a decade of Gone with the Wind's long television afterlife, though the file offers nothing to confirm it.

melody.text: Melody set records in 2024 on both measures at once, with 2,771 births and rank 91. That is worth noting because most names peak on count and rank in different years, sometimes decades apart. Growth of 34% across the decade, from a first appearance in 1914 and 111,958 births in total. The bearer list contains a nice illustration of how loosely these matches work: Lily-Rose Depp, born 1999, appears because Melody is among her given names, while Melody Thornton and the singer Melody Gardot actually go by it. Word-names drawn from music have never moved as a coherent group the way gemstone or season names have, so Melody's rise is harder to attribute to a category trend than Autumn's or Jade's.

mia.text:
Mia is a smaller name than its #5 ranking suggests — 12,113 births in 2024, its highest count since the name first peaked at 14,939 in 2015. The current figure marks a new high in rank even as the raw count sits below the 2015 peak, another example of the top of the chart getting less crowded rather than any one name surging.

The name entered SSA records later than most on this list, first appearing in 1933, and its rise has been comparatively recent and fast for something now sitting in the top five. A 10% decline over the past decade suggests it's past its steepest growth phase even while still gaining rank.

Its famous bearers cut across sport, science, and politics — soccer's Mia Hamm, astrophysicist Andrea M. Ghez, Barbadian prime minister Mia Mottley — rather than clustering in entertainment the way many short, punchy names' namesake lists tend to, which may reflect that Mia works as a standalone name in several languages rather than as a nickname import.

micah.text:
Micah barely moved over the past decade, up just 7% to 3,909 births in 2024 — count and rank both landing on fresh highs the same year, #86 nationally.

Its records start in 1946, sixty-six years after the dataset begins, a short history for a name with biblical roots.

Just two names show up as namesakes — footballer Micah Richards and comedian Katt Williams, born Micah Sierra Williams — a thin record for gains this gradual, and total US births for the name reach 129,443 since 1946.

michael.text:
Michael's scale dwarfs almost everything else in this range: 4,440,391 total US births since 1880, and it was the #1 boys' name for a long stretch through the mid-1950s, peaking at 92,786 births in a single year, 1957 — a figure that puts it in the same historical tier as James and William from the top-25 batch.

The drop-off since has been sharp by comparison: 8,189 births in 2024, down 47% from ten years prior, one of the steeper declines among the long-established names covered so far. Even so, #18 nationally is a remarkable landing spot for a name whose peak was nearly six figures in a single year.

Michael Jackson, Michael Jordan, and Michael Faraday cover music, sport, and science across three different centuries, which is typical of a name this old — its famous-bearer list reads less like a snapshot of one generation and more like a running tally across the whole 20th century.

mila.text:
Mila hit its high-water mark on both fronts in 2018 at once: 8,167 births and #14 nationally. Six years on, 5,472 births in 2024 represents a 35% gain from where it stood a decade before — one of the stronger climbs among this batch's newer, internationally-rooted names.

No famous bearers show up in the enrichment data for Mila, leaving its rise — like Aurora's and Eliana's in the third batch — without a single traceable cultural reference, even as the name has climbed steadily for over a decade.

miles.text:
Miles set fresh records in count and rank alike in 2024: 6,611 births, #37 nationally, 79% higher than a decade prior — a climb with no sign yet of the pullback seen in some of this batch's other risers.

The name has been present since 1880, a long quiet history before its recent acceleration.

Jazz musician Miles Davis anchors the name in a specific and well-known cultural reference, alongside actor Miles Teller and a rare fictional entry — Miles "Tails" Prower from the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise — a mix of real and fictional namesakes that recalls Luna's fictional-only list from the second batch, though here the real bearers outnumber the fictional one.

millie.text: Nothing else in this batch comes close to Millie's growth: 371% over ten years, roughly double the next-fastest riser. It now sits at its all-time high of 2,910 births and rank 86, having appeared in every single decade from 1880 onward while staying rare for nearly all of it — the all-time total is just 42,765. Millie Bobby Brown, born 2004, is the obvious driver; the show that made her famous arrived in 2016, and the curve responds accordingly. The other listed bearers, including the actor Millie Perkins, born 1938, and the footballer Millie Bright, predate or postdate the surge without shaping it. Diminutive names becoming formal given names is one of the strongest current patterns, and Millie is its clearest case here.

milo.text: Milo of Croton, born around 550 BCE, is by centuries the oldest namesake anywhere in this batch — a wrestler whose legend involves carrying a bull. That is a long way from the name's current profile. Milo has grown 167% over the past decade, reaching 2,988 births and rank 120, just off its 2022 high of 3,111. Although it has technically appeared in every decade since 1880, the all-time total of 41,290 is the smallest here by some distance, meaning nearly all of that history is a handful of births a year. The modern bearers — Milo Ventimiglia, born 1977, among them — do more to explain the current shape than any ancient athlete. Short, ends in a vowel, no obvious nickname needed: it fits the current preference almost exactly.

myles.text:
Myles grew 113% over the last decade, reaching a fresh high in 2024 on both fronts: 3,551 births, #99 nationally, part of a total that now stands at 61,278 since 1887.

This name's records begin in 1887, just seven years into the dataset — early, though its real growth is entirely recent.

Legal philosopher Ronald Dworkin, whose middle name was Myles, sits alongside contemporary figures — guitarist Myles Kennedy, wrestler Myles Amine — spanning academia, music, and sport with no obvious overlap between them.

naomi.text:
Naomi's rank and count peaked almost together — the rank reached #44, its best ever, in 2023, one year before the raw count reached its own high of 4,605 in 2024, a rare case of rank arriving slightly ahead of count rather than trailing it.

24% growth over the past decade is a moderate gain, well behind this batch's steeper risers like Willow or Emilia.
