Naomi Watts, Naomi Campbell, and Naomi Klein span acting, modeling, and activism across recent decades — three very different kinds of public visibility sharing one name.

natalia.text: Natalia's best rank of 79 arrived in 2021, fifteen years after its peak count of 3,587 in 2006 — higher placement on fewer births, the same field-widening effect visible throughout this batch. Today it stands at 2,498 births and rank 105, off just 11% across the decade, which makes it one of the steadier names here. Recorded from 1890, 83,141 births total. The namesakes are almost all Eastern European or Russian and span the arts: the painter Natalia Goncharova, born 1881, the writer Natalia Ginzburg, born 1916, the model Natalia Vodianova, and Natalia Dyer, born 1995. Unlike Ariana or Aaliyah, no single bearer dominates, which tends to correlate with the gentler curve Natalia has.

natalie.text:
The rank's own best, #13, came two years after the count's high point: 10,950 births in 2006, then that rank peak in 2008 — a genuine near-top-ten run, rare company for a name now sitting well outside this batch's top 50.

3,114 births and #73 is where 2024 lands, a 56% pullback since then, one of the steeper declines in this batch.

Natalie Portman and Natalie Wood anchor the name across two very different eras of Hollywood, six decades apart.

nathan.text:
2004 was Nathan's high point on both fronts at once — 14,633 births, #20 nationally. The name has been present in SSA data every year since 1880, part of a total that now stands at 584,253 births.

Twenty years on, the retreat has been substantial: 5,010 births in 2024, 44% under its count a decade prior, at #62.

Its famous-bearer list runs across acting (Nathan Fillion, Nathan Lane), theology (20th-century archbishop Nathan Söderblom), and comedy (George Burns, born Nathan Birnbaum) — four very different careers sharing one name across roughly a century of public life.

nathaniel.text: Nathaniel has lost 42% over the decade, easing to 2,511 births and rank 144, well below the 6,813 it managed in 2002 and the rank of 60 it held in 1998. That is a moderate decline by the standards of this batch, and its 285,643 births are spread widely enough since 1880 that the name has never been tied to one generation the way Evan or Connor is. Nathaniel Hawthorne, born 1804, is the anchor, though the file lists his occupation as science fiction writer, which would have surprised him. Ralph Fiennes and Jacob Elordi both carry it as a middle name, and the rapper Nate Dogg was born Nathaniel Hale. The formal four-syllable register is out of fashion generally, and Nathaniel is declining roughly in line with that.

nicholas.text: No name in this batch has fallen further. Nicholas peaked at 29,161 births in 1995 and reached rank 5 in 1999; it now records 3,025 births at rank 118. That is a 55% decline over the past ten years alone, and roughly a tenth of its peak volume. The all-time total of 926,036 is the second-largest here, behind only George — this was a genuinely dominant name for a long stretch. The bearer list is heavily contemporary, with Nicholas Hoult, born 1989, and Nick Jonas, born 1992, alongside Nick Nolte. Adrien Brody appears on a middle-name match. What the numbers describe is a name that saturated: extremely common for parents born in the seventies and eighties, and now carrying exactly the generational stamp that makes a name hard to choose.

noah.text:
Noah has held a top-two US ranking almost continuously since 2013, and its 2024 count of 20,337 is close to its all-time high, up a modest 5% over the past decade — a slower climb than Liam's but a steadier one, without the swings that hit most biblical names in recent decades.

What sets Noah apart from most names this popular is its span: it appears in SSA records going all the way back to 1880, present in every decade since, long before its recent surge. That kind of continuous low-level use before a breakout is rare among current top-10 names, most of which were essentially absent before the 1980s or 1990s.

The famous-bearer list is unusually varied for a name this size — a historian (Yuval Noah Harari), a 18th-century lexicographer (Noah Webster), a Grammy-winning musician (Adam Levine), and a sprinter (Noah Lyles) — spanning centuries and fields rather than clustering around one recent cultural moment, which tracks with a name whose popularity was already broad before it became the biggest name in the country.

nolan.text:
Nolan's count and rank diverged by eight years: 5,739 births in 2015 was the raw-count high, while #57, the best rank, only arrived in 2023 — shorter than Zoe's twelve-year gap or Joshua's thirteen-year one from earlier batches, but part of the same general pattern.

The ten-year change is nearly flat, down just 6% to 4,888 births in 2024.

Video game pioneer Nolan Bushnell anchors the name in 1970s tech history, alongside younger entertainment figures Nolan Gould and Nolan North — an odd pairing of industries that don't usually share a namesake.

nora.text:
Nora's 2024 numbers are its best yet on both fronts: 6,128 births, #22 nationally, up 29% from a decade earlier — a more modest gain than fast risers like Maverick or Eliana, but consistently upward with no sign of reversal.

Present in SSA data since 1880, the name spent well over a century in minor use, similar in shape to Hazel and Violet, before its own recent climb.

Its famous-bearer list spans essayist Nora Ephron, actor Awkwafina (born Nora Lum), and Hugo-winning novelist N. K. Jemisin (born Nora Keita Jemisin) — writers and performers across several decades rather than a single generational cluster.

nova.text:
Nova's climb over the past decade, 344%, ranks among the largest in this batch, trailing only Enzo and Lainey. Both its count and rank reached fresh territory recently — 5,044 births in 2024, though its actual peak, 5,920, came two years earlier in 2022.

What's unusual here is the data history: first recorded in 1885, just five years into the dataset, meaning Nova has technically existed as a US name for well over a century despite reading as an entirely modern invention.

The enrichment data offers no famous bearers to explain any of this — the name's popularity, like Aurora's in an earlier batch, isn't traceable to any single documented figure.

oakley.text: Oakley has grown 419% in ten years, the second-largest gain in this batch, and its history is the most broken of any name here: recorded in 1913, then nothing at all across the 1930s, 1940s, 1950s, 1960s and 1970s — five straight decades missing — before it returned. Current figures are 1,894 births at rank 157, an all-time high on count. Just 24,104 births in total, the smallest cumulative figure in this batch by a distance. The single listed namesake is the rapper Central Cee, born 1998, whose given name is Oakley Caesar-Su, which almost certainly postdates the American rise rather than causing it. Annie Oakley, the obvious historical association, is absent from the file entirely — a gap worth knowing about before treating these lists as complete.

oliver.text:
Oliver's 2024 count of 15,343 is its highest ever and represents 62% growth over the past decade, the strongest ten-year gain of any name in the current US top five. It first cracked the top three in 2019 and has held there since, a rapid rise for a name that spent most of the 20th century well outside the top 50.

The name has been in continuous use since 1880, giving it a longer paper trail than its recent popularity might suggest. Its most prominent historical bearer, Oliver Cromwell, sits at the opposite end of the name's public image from its current soft, storybook-adjacent appeal — a reminder that a name's associations can shift entirely across four centuries of use.

Oliver's growth has tracked closely with Liam's and Noah's rather than following its own separate trend, all three -er/-ah ending names rising together through the 2010s and 2020s. That kind of clustered movement, several similar-sounding names climbing in parallel, is more typical of a broader sound preference than any one name's individual appeal.

olivia.text:
Olivia's chart tells a less obvious story than its current #1 ranking suggests. Births actually peaked in 2014 at 19,836 and have fallen 26% over the past decade, down to 14,718 in 2024. It holds the top spot not because it's still climbing but because names in general have spread across a wider field of choices, so the #1 name today needs a smaller share of the total than it did a generation ago.

Olivia has been given to American girls in every decade since the SSA started counting in 1880, which is unusual longevity for a name with no single film, show, or celebrity tied to its rise. Judi Dench, Olivia de Havilland, and Olivia Rodrigo are all connected to the name but from different eras and different fields entirely, which is more likely a symptom of the name's staying power than a cause of it.

The practical case for Olivia hasn't really changed: three syllables that read as formal on paper, a soft opening sound, and a built-in nickname (Liv, Ollie) for parents who want options later. That combination of stability and flexibility is probably why it's held the #1 rank since 2019 even as the raw count declines.

owen.text:
Owen's rank has fallen further and faster than its raw numbers alone would suggest: it peaked at #18 in 2022 but had dropped to #26 by 2024, an eight-place slide in just two years, even though the count decline over the full decade is a comparatively mild 17%. That gap between a sharp recent rank drop and a gentler long-term count trend is unusual in this batch.

The name shows up in every decade of SSA data since 1880, a long and steady history before its 2016 peak of 10,302 births.

Its famous-bearer list mixes science (Nobel physicist Owen Willans Richardson, Owen Chamberlain) with entertainment (Owen Wilson) and sport (Owen Hargreaves) — a broad spread that doesn't cluster around any single field the way Camila's or Dylan's namesake lists do.

paisley.text:
By 2015, Paisley's count and its rank had both reached their peak — 5,089 births, #45 nationally — before a 21% pullback over the following ten years left it at 3,542 births and #61 by 2024, one of the milder declines in this batch.

The name's history starts in 1966, roughly the same era as Zoey's own late entry into the data.

No famous bearers show up in the enrichment data, leaving both the mid-2010s rise and the recent pullback without a single documented cultural anchor.

parker.text:
Parker sits noticeably lower in this batch than its neighbors: #97 nationally in 2024, the only name here outside the top 50, with 3,605 births — down 37% over the past decade from a rank peak of #72 in 2015, itself only modest by this batch's standards.

Parker's own SSA data reaches back to 1880 too, a long, mostly quiet history before a brief mid-2010s rise that never reached the heights of names like Mason or Carter.

Its famous-bearer list mixes film (Cliff Robertson, whose middle name was Parker), music (mandolinist Parker Posey), and sport (basketball's Cade Cunningham, middle name Parker) — three different fields, none of them producing a namesake prominent or recent enough to have driven the name's modest 2010s bump.

penelope.text:
Penelope's rank reached its best-ever mark, #21, in 2022, three years after its raw count peaked at 6,733 births in 2019 — count falling while rank still climbed, the same pattern seen in Scarlett.

5,741 births in 2024 is only 13% more than a decade before — a modest gain next to this batch's bigger risers like Rowan or Thiago.

Unusually, no famous bearers are listed for Penelope at all, despite its flagged French origin and its long presence in Greek mythology through Odysseus's wife — a gap between cultural weight and documented namesakes that Aurora and Eliana also showed in the third batch.

quinn.text:
Almost no net change for Quinn over the past decade, up a mere 5% — though the count and rank moved on different schedules: 3,648 births was the count's high, back in 2016, while the rank didn't hit its own best, #73, until six years later, in 2022.

This name enters the record in 1948, sixty-eight years into the dataset.

Actor Ciara Bravo is the only name the enrichment data offers, her career starting well after Quinn's own 2016 high.

raelynn.text: RaeLynn has grown 95% over the decade, reaching 2,412 births at rank 113, a little below its 2022 peak. No bearers are recorded and no origin is listed, which for a name at this volume is becoming a familiar pattern in this batch — Juniper, Malachi and Hadley are all in the same position. Recorded from 1947 with 32,373 births in total. Structurally it is a compound, Rae plus Lynn, and belongs to a naming tradition strongest in the American South that has been generating these fusions for decades. The country singer RaeLynn, who rose to attention in 2012, is not in the file despite the timing lining up better than most attributions that are.

remi.text: Remi has grown 357% across the decade, though it has already come off its 2022 high of 2,389 births and rank 118, now recording 1,987 at rank 145. That combination — enormous ten-year growth alongside a recent dip — makes it one of the harder names here to read. Of French origin, recorded from 1963, 24,701 births total. All three listed bearers are French men: the philosopher Rémi Brague, born 1947, the footballer Rémi Garde, and the YouTuber Rémi Gaillard, born 1975. The American usage is predominantly female, so the file describes a different name from the one the numbers track — a mismatch that recurs wherever a name has crossed both language and sex.

riley.text:
Riley's ten-year percentage change, -3%, makes the decline look almost flat, but that number hides a sharper real story: the count spiked to a peak of 7,159 in 2016, the same year the rank hit its best-ever #22, before falling to just 4,644 births and #42 by 2024 — a steep drop from the mid-decade high that the simple ten-year comparison mostly cancels out.

The name entered SSA data in 1923, decades before most of this batch's recent arrivals like Maverick or Eliana.

Its famous-bearer list runs almost entirely adult-entertainment and film — Riley Reid, Riley Keough, Riley Steele — alongside one unrelated historical figure, Vice President Thomas R. Marshall (whose middle name was Riley), an odd mix that doesn't map cleanly onto the name's current use for young children.

river.text:
River sits well below most of its neighbors in this batch: #112 nationally in 2024, the lowest rank of any name here, with 3,138 births — down from a peak of 3,503 in 2021, when its rank also hit its own best, #105, the following year.

Despite that modest current standing, the ten-year growth rate, 152%, is substantial, and this name's records begin in 1971, more recent than most but earlier than Lainey's or Madison's late arrivals.

Actor River Phoenix, who died in 1993, is the only bearer in the enrichment data — a specific, well-known namesake for a name that remains this batch's smallest by current rank despite genuine recent growth.

robert.text:
4,866,007 total US births make Robert one of this dataset's largest names by history — behind only James's and John's even bigger totals, just ahead of Michael's and William's. Its rank hit #1 in 1924; the count itself didn't peak until 1947, at 91,654 births — 23 years separating the two records.

2024's count, 3,785, sits 43% below its own count from a decade back, at #90 nationally — a steep percentage fall for a name whose historical scale rivals the very largest in this dataset.

Bob Dylan, born Robert Allen Zimmerman, and Bob Marley, born Robert Nesta Marley, keep the shortened form alive in music; Robert Louis Stevenson anchors the full name in 19th-century literature.

roman.text:
Roman's 2024 count, 5,474 births, is a new high alongside its best-ever rank, #52 — a 57% climb over the past decade, a solid but not extreme gain compared to this batch's steeper risers like Ivy or Ezekiel.

The name has technically been recorded since 1882, though it stayed minor for over thirteen decades before this recent run.

Film director Roman Polanski and businessman Roman Abramovich give the name a contemporary, mostly European set of namesakes, joined by novelist Romain Gary — a cluster that skews recent and international rather than reaching back through American history the way Charles's or Joshua's lists do.

rory.text: Rory sits at its record on both measures, 1,594 births and rank 226, each set in 2024, after growing 113% across the decade. That rank is the weakest anywhere in this slice, which makes the pairing unusual — a record year that still leaves it well outside the top two hundred. That combination describes a name on the way up rather than one that has arrived. First recorded in 1933, 46,310 births in total. The bearers are strongly Irish and Scottish: the guitarist Rory Gallagher, born 1948, and the golfer Rory McIlroy, born 1989, alongside Rory Culkin. Like Declan it belongs to the Irish cohort, but where Declan is falling from its peak, Rory has not obviously reached one yet.

rose.text: Rose is up 40% across the decade despite having peaked in 1917 at 9,783 births and ranked 14 as far back as 1911. That combination — deep history, genuine current growth — is unusual, and Rose manages it partly because it never fully disappeared: 500,276 births since 1880, the third-largest total here, accumulated steadily rather than in a burst. The current figures are 2,376 births and rank 115. Every listed bearer holds it second rather than first: Emilia Clarke, born 1986, Lily Allen, Emma Roberts, Sienna Miller, Claudia Cardinale. That is not an accident of the data. Rose is overwhelmingly used as a middle name in practice, so its first-name count understates its real presence by a wide margin.

rowan.text:
No name in this batch grew faster than Rowan except Thiago: 4,647 births at #71 in 2024, both fresh highs, 200% above where the name stood a decade earlier.

SSA records for this name start in 1916, though it stayed a minor presence for nearly a century before this recent surge.

The famous-bearer list here is unusually varied for a name this size — 19th-century mathematician William Rowan Hamilton, actor Rowan Atkinson, and the Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams all carry the name as either a first or middle name, spanning science, comedy, and the clergy in a way that doesn't cluster around one field the way Cooper's thin list does.

ruby.text:
Ruby is essentially unchanged across the last ten years, gaining only 3% to reach 3,517 births in 2024. Its real story is much older: the rank peaked first, #22 in 1911, while the raw count didn't reach its own high, 8,406 births, until 1924 — 13 years apart, with total births now standing at 376,074 since 1880.

Barbara Stanwyck and Ruby Dee anchor it in classic Hollywood; radio astronomer Ruby Payne-Scott gives it real scientific weight too, active from the 1940s onward.

ryan.text:
29,909 births in 1985 was Ryan's high point by raw count; #11, the rank's own best, showed up the following year. Both numbers have been sliding since — 3,892 births and #87 by 2024, a 57% drop over just the last ten years, the steepest fall in this batch.

Nearly a million US babies have carried this name since 1906, when it first entered the data — later than most Irish-origin names of comparable size.

Ryan Gosling and Ryan Reynolds, born just four years apart, cover most of the name's current public image between them.

ryder.text: Ryder has the lowest rank in this batch at 134, and the trajectory explains why: down 35% over the decade from a 2015 high of 4,163 births to 2,694, with its best rank of 95 reached back in 2014. First recorded in 1960, all-time total 66,224. It arrived as part of the occupational-surname wave alongside Hunter and Parker, and it is leaving on the same schedule. The listed bearers are marginal — the cyclist Ryder Hesjedal, born 1980, and the actor Abby Ryder Fortson, born 2008, whose middle name it is. Neither shaped the curve. What lifted Ryder was an association with motion and toughness that reads, a decade on, as distinctly of its moment, which is the recurring risk with names chosen mainly for connotation.

rylee.text: Rylee's best placing of 98 came in 2021, eleven years after its highest count of 2,984 in 2010 — the pattern of rising in rank while falling in volume that recurs throughout this dataset. It now stands at 2,229 births and rank 125, down 20% over ten years. Recorded from 1980, 72,330 births total, and no namesakes listed. The larger issue is spelling: Riley, Ryleigh, Rileigh and Rylie all compete for the same sound, and Riley in particular is far more common, so this line captures a minority of the children who answer to it. Among names in this batch with no attached person, Rylee is unusual in having already peaked — most of the others are still climbing.

sadie.text:
3,729 births in 2024 puts Sadie 23% below its count from a decade earlier — a milder fall than several names nearby in this range. 2014 was the year both measures peaked together: 4,870 births, #46 nationally.

The name's own records stretch back to the dataset's 1880 start, and its total US births reach 145,728 over that span.

Stranger Things actor Sadie Sink is the standout contemporary namesake; 1940s film star Joan Leslie rounds out a short list spanning eight decades.

sage.text: Sage has grown 135% over the decade, currently 1,987 births at rank 146, just under its 2022 records. It carries no listed origin, which is fitting for a name that operates simultaneously as a herb, a virtue and a surname without committing to any of them. The record begins in 1963 and totals 43,653 births. The two namesakes are both minor and both American: Sage Stallone, born 1976, and the snowboarder Sage Kotsenburg. Neither explains the curve. What does explain it is category momentum — Sage sits with Sawyer and Rowan in the group of short, nature-adjacent, sex-ambiguous names that have been rising steadily for fifteen years. The risk with that cohort is the one Blake illustrates immediately above: unisex names rarely hold their position for long.

samuel.text:
Samuel's best-ever rank, #17, was already achieved in 1880 — the very first year the SSA data covers — meaning by the time this dataset starts recording, the name had already peaked positionally and everything since has been a name holding on rather than climbing. Its raw count peaked much later, 14,813 births in 2001, but even that high point never matched the name's relative dominance from 1880.

Today's 8,310 births in 2024 is down 25% from a decade earlier, a decline shared with several long-standing names in this range rather than anything specific to Samuel.

The famous-bearer list runs almost entirely through 18th- and 19th-century letters — lexicographer Samuel Johnson, poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge, telegraph inventor Samuel Morse — with Mark Twain (born Samuel Clemens) as the closest thing to a household name. That's a narrower, more literary cluster than most names this size carry, most of them born well before the 20th century.

santiago.text:
Santiago set new highs in both count and rank in the same year, 2024 — 7,407 births at #29 nationally, 116% higher than ten years earlier — with no indication yet of the kind of pullback already visible in Leo or Owen.

SSA records for this name stretch back to 1880, a long quiet history before this recent climb, similar in shape to Elias and Asher: old roots, recent breakout.

Its famous-bearer list is dense with Spanish-language achievement across very different fields — neuroscientist Santiago Ramón y Cajal, architect Santiago Calatrava, footballer Federico Valverde (whose full name includes Santiago) — a cluster of intellectual and athletic figures that fits the name's Spanish origin more tightly than most of its English-origin neighbors in this batch manage with theirs.

sarah.text: At 1,099,063 births, Sarah is the largest name in this entire batch — more than a million American girls, and roughly a quarter more than Anna. It reached rank 3 in 1993 and its highest count of 28,488 in 1982. Today: 2,697 births, rank 95, down 43% over ten years. That trajectory is the standard fate of a name that was genuinely ubiquitous for a generation; there is no way back to the top while everyone associates it with people now in their forties. The bearers span centuries and fields — Sarah Bernhardt, born 1844, Sarah Jessica Parker, Sarah Michelle Gellar — and Jane Wyman, born 1917, appears through her birth name Sarah Jane Mayfield. Ubiquity and desirability are not the same thing, and Sarah demonstrates the gap.

savannah.text: Savannah has fallen 55% across the decade, down to 2,490 births and rank 107 from the 7,101 it recorded in 2000, its best placing of 30 having come in 2006. Like Brooklyn it is a place-name with a tightly bounded life — 189,552 births, overwhelmingly concentrated between 1990 and 2010 despite the name being recorded from 1880. The single listed bearer is spelled differently from the name itself, Savanna Samson, born 1967, which makes the file effectively empty. Southern place-names had a strong run through the nineties and have receded together since; what remains is a name that reads as distinctly of that period, which is the recurring difficulty with choosing any of them now.

sawyer.text:
#132 nationally, with 2,756 births — Sawyer trails nearly everything else in this batch by current standing. 2015 was its actual peak on both fronts: 4,271 births, #94, the same year — followed by an unusually steep 23% decline over the past decade for a name still this far down the chart.

The record here is patchy: first appearing in 1913, then gone for decades until it resumes in the 1970s, a longer gap than Gael's own mid-century absence.

No famous bearers appear anywhere in the enrichment data — both the mid-2010s rise and the fall since remain undocumented by any single cultural reference.

scarlett.text:
Scarlett shows an unusual split: its raw count peaked back in 2017 at 7,719 births, but its best-ever rank, #14, didn't arrive until five years later, in 2022 — the count fell while the rank kept improving, meaning competing names dropped faster than Scarlett did.

First recorded in 1937, the name has a shorter data history than most names this popular, entering nearly six decades after the dataset begins.

Scarlett Johansson dominates the name's public association, joined by an unexpected second entry — Julia Louis-Dreyfus, whose middle name is Scarlett — a namesake list built almost entirely around one generation of actresses rather than spanning centuries the way Emily's does.

sebastian.text:
Sebastian has moved in a narrow band for nearly a decade: it peaked in 2016 at 10,308 births, held its best-ever rank of #13 in 2022, and sits at 8,562 in 2024, down a modest 8% over the past decade — one of the more stable trajectories in this batch, without a sharp rise or fall.

The name dates to 1881 in SSA records and has been present in every decade since, a long, quiet history similar to Sebastian's fellow German-origin name Oliver, though without Oliver's recent acceleration.

Johann Sebastian Bach anchors the name to a very different era and field than its other famous bearers — Formula One's Sebastian Vettel, actor Rowan Atkinson (born Rowan Sebastian Atkinson), and former Austrian chancellor Sebastian Kurz — a spread across three centuries and several countries that may help explain why the name has stayed steady rather than tracking any single trend.

serenity.text: Serenity peaked on count and rank together in 2013, reaching 4,471 births alongside rank 52. A 46% slide since leaves it on 2,342 births and rank 117. Its history begins in 1972 and amounts to 75,336 births, with neither origin nor bearers on file. It belongs to the virtue-name tradition alongside Trinity and Destiny, a group that rose sharply through the 1990s and 2000s and has been receding together ever since. The absence of any namesake is characteristic rather than an oversight: these names are chosen for the word's meaning, not for anyone who held it. That makes them unusually vulnerable to shifts in taste, because there is no historical anchor holding them in place when the fashion moves on.

shiloh.text: Shiloh holds the lowest rank in this batch at 260, on 1,216 births in 2024, which is nonetheless its best year on both measures after 152% growth across the decade. Recorded from 1969 with 22,186 births total. Of Hebrew origin, and like Zion it is a biblical place rather than a biblical person, which puts it in a small category with distinct behaviour. One bearer is listed, the actor Shiloh Fernandez, born 1985. Absent from the file, and almost certainly more consequential, is Shiloh Jolie-Pitt, born 2006, whose birth generated the kind of coverage that reliably moves a name — the American curve begins climbing shortly afterwards.

silas.text:
4,108 births made 2024 Silas's best year on record — though the rank actually hit its own peak, #81, a year earlier in 2023, an unusual case of rank leading rather than trailing.

40% growth over the past decade lands Silas well below Theo's or Walker's much bigger jumps, though still solidly positive. Total US births for this name reach 70,949 since 1880, a modest but steady historical base.

Communist journalist John Reed carried Silas as a middle name; actor Silas Weir Mitchell is the closest thing to a direct namesake here.

skylar.text: Skylar peaked on both measures during 2015, reaching 5,294 births alongside rank 42. A 54% surrender since drops it to 2,186 births and rank 134. Recorded from 1974, 103,743 births, no listed origin. Two bearers appear, the musician Skylar Grey, born 1986, and the actor Skylar Astin, and neither predates the rise. The name is genuinely unisex and additionally fragmented across Skyler, Schuyler and Skye, so the counted string is a poor guide to how often the sound is used. Its arc closely tracks Blake's — another unisex name that climbed hard and fell hard — which reinforces the pattern that names without a settled sex tend to have shorter, sharper lives.

sofia.text:
Sofia — this spelling, distinct from "Sophia" — is a useful contrast to its more common cousin: both are declining in raw count, but Sofia just reached its best-ever national rank, #10, in 2024, even as its count fell 16% over the decade to 8,094. Like Amelia in the top-25 batch, it's benefiting from the general spreading-out of the naming pool rather than any growth of its own.

It first appears in SSA records in 1881, only a year after Sophia, and the two spellings have tracked each other loosely ever since without ever fully merging into one dominant form.

Sofia Loren, Sofia Coppola, and Sofia Carson span film across nearly a century, along with the enrichment data's cross-listing of Sophia Loren under this shorter spelling — a reminder that spelling variants of the same name often share famous bearers in ways strict alphabetical splitting doesn't fully capture.

sophia.text:
Sophia's trajectory is one of the sharper reversals in the current top ten: it was the #1 girls' name as recently as 2011, peaking at 22,335 births in 2012, and now sits at #6 with 12,088 in 2024 — a 35% drop over just the past decade, among the sharper reversals in this batch though not the sharpest.

It's been recorded since 1880, giving it more than a century of continuous use before its 2010s surge, and the name carries genuine historical range: Sophia of Hanover was an actual 17th-century royal, distinct from more recently invented "sophia" variants used in branding or fiction.

The decline pattern here looks similar to Emma's and Isabella's — all three peaked in the early-to-mid 2010s and have fallen by roughly a third since — suggesting a cohort of once-dominant, classically-toned names that rose together and are now cooling together, likely displaced by shorter or less familiar alternatives among parents looking for something that reads as less common.

sophie.text:
Sophie is nearly flat, gaining only 5% across the last ten years, settling at 3,574 births in 2024. 2011 was the peak year for both count and rank at once — 4,732 births, #51 nationally.

This name has been present across the dataset's entire span, back to 1880, with total US births reaching 134,691.

Catherine the Great of Russia and mathematician Sophie Germain anchor it in 18th-century European history; Game of Thrones actor Sophie Turner keeps it current today, alongside film star Sophie Marceau.

stella.text:
Barely anything changed for Stella over the past decade — up just 1%, to 4,264 births in 2024, one of the smallest ten-year moves covered anywhere in this dataset. 2018 was its high-water mark: 5,163 births, #38 nationally.

This name's records stretch back to 1880, quiet through most of the 20th century before its 2010s climb.

Fashion designer Stella McCartney and actor Stella Adler keep the name visible today; Australian author Miles Franklin, born Stella Maria Sarah Miles Franklin in the 1870s, gives it an older literary root few would expect.

stetson.text: Stetson is up 756% across ten years, the steepest climb anywhere in this slice and one of the steepest on the site outside the two four-figure outliers. Its history is threadbare to match: recorded in 1930, then missing entirely through the 1940s, 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, and 13,016 births in total across everything since. There are no namesakes of any kind. What there is, unmistakably, is a hat — the John B. Stetson Company has been making them since the 1860s, and the name functions as a piece of Western Americana rather than as a personal name with any lineage. It reached 2,328 births and rank 155 in 2024, both records. Names carried by a single cultural association tend to move fast in both directions.

sutton.text: Sutton carries the weakest placing anywhere in this slice at 197, despite growing 332% over the decade and setting records in 2024 with 1,559 births. A record year that still leaves a name outside the top hundred and fifty describes something arriving rather than something established. Recorded from 1963, just 17,295 births in total. The single listed bearer is the actor Sutton Foster, born 1975, who has been prominent on Broadway for two decades and is a more plausible source than most single-namesake attributions in these batches. Like Beckett and Hadley it is a surname with no personal history behind it in American use, and like them it is being chosen for shape rather than meaning.

tatum.text:
Just 1,497 births in 2024 — the smallest count of any name covered here — though that's still a record for Tatum, matched by a fresh best-ever rank, #205, up 79% from a decade earlier.

Records here start in 1966, well past the dataset's halfway point, and this name's overall total comes to 38,455 births.

Actor Tatum O'Neal was born in 1963, four decades before the enrichment data's other namesake, singer Tate McRae — an unusually wide generational gap for such a small name.

theo.text:
647% — the biggest ten-year gain in this batch, though the fifth batch's Lainey still holds the overall dataset record at 901%. Theo's own peak, on both fronts at once, landed in 2023: 4,137 births, #78 nationally, easing only slightly to 4,110 and #80 by 2024.

Just 35,340 US births total trace to this name since 1880 — a small enough base that the huge percentage growth makes more sense, the same shape seen in Thiago's and Lainey's own surges.

Two footballers, both under the accented spelling Théo, are the only entries in the enrichment data: Théo Hernandez and, oddly, 19th-century painter Théo van Rysselberghe.

theodore.text:
Theodore's 2024 count of 12,011 is its highest ever, and the 272% rise over the past decade is the largest ten-year gain of any name in this batch by a wide margin — a genuine breakout rather than a gradual climb, going from a niche choice to the #4 boys' name in barely more than ten years.

The name has been present in SSA data since 1880 but spent nearly all of that history well outside the top ranks, making its recent jump unusually steep for a name with no single obvious trigger — no blockbuster character or celebrity baby tied to the surge that the data can confirm.

Its nickname options (Theo, Teddy) likely help explain part of the appeal: a formal, old-fashioned full name that still offers a soft, casual short form, a combination that several other currently rising names (Theodore, Sebastian to a lesser extent) share and that seems to be a stronger predictor of growth right now than the formal name's sound alone.

thiago.text:
Thiago posted the biggest percentage jump of any name across all four batches so far: 564%, taking it from a near-nonexistent presence to 5,289 births in 2024, with its rank hitting a fresh best, #55, the same year.

Much of that is a base-rate effect — the name's total births since it first entered the data, in 1986, run to just 29,375, the smallest total of any name covered in this batch, well below every other entry here, and its history spans only five decades rather than the thirteen or fourteen most other names in this range carry.

The famous-bearer list here is unusually uniform: five professional footballers, all Brazilian, all born within a decade of each other — Thiago Silva, Thiago Alcântara, Thiago Motta, Thiago Neves, Thiago Cionek — a namesake cluster with no equivalent elsewhere in this batch.

thomas.text:
Thomas's rank peaked at #8 in 1880, the very first year of this dataset — the same early-peak pattern seen in James, John, and Samuel — while its raw count didn't reach its high of 48,650 births until 1952, seven decades later.

The recent trend is unusually flat for a name this old: 6,576 births in 2024 is just 7% below its count from ten years earlier, one of the mildest ten-year moves in this entire batch.

Thomas Edison, Thomas Jefferson, and Thomas Hobbes span invention, politics, and philosophy across four centuries — a namesake list with the same kind of long historical reach as John's or David's from earlier batches, fitting for a name whose own data history runs the full length of the dataset.

valentina.text:
2024 brought Valentina to a fresh high on both fronts at once: 4,438 births, #47 nationally, up 60% from its count ten years earlier.

The name's data history starts in 1897, seventeen years into the dataset. It sat at low volume through most of the 1900s before this recent run.

Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space, anchors the name in a specific and singular historical achievement — a namesake with more individual weight than most of the loosely-connected lists elsewhere in this batch.

victoria.text:
12,926 births in 1993 was Victoria's peak count; #16, its best rank, arrived five years afterward in 1998. Since then: a 47% slide over the last decade, settling at 4,267 births and #48 nationally by 2024.

Over half a million US births carry this name since 1880, and its royal weight runs deep — Queen Victoria of the United Kingdom was born in 1819, more than a century before the American name's own high point.

Victoria Beckham keeps it current in fashion; Sweden's Crown Princess Victoria keeps it current in monarchy.

vincent.text:
1962's 6,161 births marked Vincent's count peak; the rank followed four years afterward, hitting #58 in 1966. What's followed since has been unusually stable for this batch — just a 16% dip over the last decade, landing at 3,158 births and #111 in 2024.

Overall, 361,416 people have been given this name since 1880.

Vincent van Gogh anchors it in 19th-century art; Frank Zappa and Jon Voight, both born Vincent, carry it under different stage identities in music and film.

violet.text:
Both the count and the rank for Violet hit new highs in 2024 — 6,972 births at #15, up 66% from a decade earlier — with nothing in the data suggesting a turn yet.

Present in SSA records since 1880, the name stayed a minor presence for more than a hundred years before this recent run.

Its enrichment list is unusually scientific for a flower name: economist Joan Robinson, radio astronomer Ruby Payne-Scott, and Titanic survivor and nurse Violet Jessop, none of them entertainment figures, a different profile than most of this batch's fast risers, whose namesake lists tend to skew toward actors and musicians.

vivian.text:
Barely moved at all: Vivian is up just 1% across the last ten years, to 3,088 births in 2024. Its real high point came a century earlier — 1920 brought both measures to their peak at once, 4,128 births and #64 nationally.

This name's own total reaches 227,375 births since 1880.

Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett's middle name is Vivian; street photographer Vivian Maier, whose work was discovered only after her death, gives the name a very different kind of 20th-century legacy.

walker.text:
Only Theo grew faster than Walker in this batch: 285% over the past decade. 4,248 births and #78 arrived together in 2022, before easing to 4,023 and #82 by 2024.

Records for this name go back to the dataset's 1880 start, quiet through most of the 20th century before the recent surge.

George W. Bush, whose middle name is Walker, sits alongside novelist Walker Percy and photographer Walker Evans — three men who all carried it as a middle name, not a first one.

waylon.text:
Waylon's 4,878 births in 2024 runs 225% ahead of its count a decade earlier, just short of the name's actual peak, 4,918, set two years earlier in 2022.

The name's data history stretches back to 1911, though it stayed at low volume through most of the 1900s.

Country musician Waylon Jennings is the clear namesake here — a specific, well-known figure rather than the documentation gap seen with fellow risers Nova or Lainey elsewhere in this batch, though whether his fame from decades ago explains a 2020s surge is something the birth data alone can't confirm.

wesley.text:
5,144 births in 2024 marks Wesley's best year yet, and the rank moved in lockstep — #58, also a fresh high, up 64% from where the name stood ten years before.

This name's SSA history stretches all the way back to the dataset's start in 1880, though its recent gain is entirely a 21st-century story.

Wesley Snipes and Wes Craven anchor the shortened form in film, while Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry (born Eugene Wesley Roddenberry) gives the full name an unexpected science-fiction connection.

weston.text:
2024 brought Weston a fresh high on both measures at once: 4,660 births, #70 nationally, up 57% from a decade before — a moderate gain compared to this batch's bigger risers like Enzo or Nova.

The name has technically been recorded since 1882, though it stayed at low volume for over a century before this recent climb.

Its enrichment data lists just two bearers, footballer Weston McKennie and musician Porter Robinson (born Porter Robinson Weston) — a thin namesake record for a name whose growth has been entirely recent.

william.text:
William's scale dwarfs nearly every other name in this batch: 4,205,026 total US births since 1880, and it held the #2 national rank in 1880 itself, the earliest year in the data — meaning the name was already firmly established well over a century before this dataset begins its count.

Its 1947 peak of 67,001 births in a single year reflects an era when a much smaller set of names covered most babies born. William now ranks #10 with 10,596 births in 2024, 37% below its count from ten years prior, but that has to be read against a name that's simply operating in a far more fragmented naming landscape than it once was.

The famous-bearer list underscores the name's long reach — William Shakespeare, Stephen Hawking, Bertrand Russell — literary and scientific figures spanning five centuries. Few currently top-ten names carry that kind of unbroken historical weight while still ranking among America's most-used names today.

willow.text:
Willow's rise, 93% over the past decade, has already passed its peak by one measure: the raw count topped out in 2021 at 5,193, while the rank kept climbing for another year, reaching #37 in 2022, before both eased to 4,653 births and #41 by 2024.

This name's records begin in 1890, a decade later than most names in this dataset, though it stayed minor for most of the twentieth century before this recent run.

Willow Smith, born in 2000, is the clearest namesake — young enough that her own career and the name's later surge are roughly contemporaries rather than one obviously causing the other.

wyatt.text:
Wyatt peaked in 2017 on both fronts — 9,726 births and its best-ever rank, #25 — then eased to #38 by 2024 with 6,581 births, a 26% ten-year decline that's milder than Carter's or Jackson's.

Recorded since 1880, the name spent well over a century in minor use before its 2010s rise.

Wyatt Earp anchors the name firmly in 19th-century American frontier history, a specific and singular reference point that hardly any other name in this batch carries — most, like Carter or Maverick, have either no dominant historical namesake or several competing ones rather than one figure this closely associated with the name itself.

xavier.text:
2007 doubled as Xavier's high-water mark on both fronts: 6,560 births, #68 nationally. What followed was a 30% pullback over the next ten years, settling at 3,337 births and #102 by 2024.

This name first shows up six years into the dataset, in 1886, and its total births now run to 157,909 over that span.

Footballer Xavi Hernández and Luxembourg's prime minister, Xavier Bettel, keep it visible in European sport and politics; actor Gérard Depardieu carries it as a middle name.

zion.text: Zion has one of the most broken histories on this site: recorded in 1917, then nothing across the 1920s, 1930s, 1940s, 1950s and 1960s, before resuming. Five decades absent, matching Oakley's gap almost exactly. It is now up 59% over ten years, at 2,359 births and rank 151, marginally below its 2023 records. Cumulative total 51,273. The two bearers are both athletes born this century — Zion Williamson, born 2000, and the goalkeeper Zion Suzuki — meaning they are products of the name's revival rather than its cause. As a biblical place-name rather than a person-name, Zion sits slightly apart from Malachi and Jonah, and its usage patterns look correspondingly different.

zoe.text:
Zoe carries one of the longer gaps in this batch between its count peak and its rank peak: the raw count topped out in 2012 at 6,466 births, but the rank didn't reach its own best-ever mark, #29, until 2024 — twelve years later, second only to Joshua's thirteen-year lag elsewhere in this batch.

The pct change over the past decade is nearly flat, down just 3% to 5,719 births in 2024.

No origin and no famous bearers appear in the enrichment data at all, leaving Zoe's steady, quiet persistence — present since 1880, never spiking, never collapsing — without any obvious cultural explanation the data can offer.

zoey.text:
Zoey's fall matches Jaxon's almost exactly: 52% over the past decade, versus his 53%. Both its count and rank peaked in 2012 — 7,481 births, #20 nationally — before easing to 3,600 and #59 by 2024.

Records for this spelling start in 1967, decades later than the more traditional "Zoe" spelling covered in an earlier batch.

Actor Zoey Deutch is the only bearer in the enrichment data, her career beginning right around the name's own 2012 peak — no other namesake shows up anywhere in the record.
